chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Lord Bardolph.]
LORD BARDOLPH. Who's guarding the gate here? Hello!
[The Porter opens the gate.]
Where is the Earl?
PORTER. Who shall I say you are?
LORD BARDOLPH. Tell the Earl that Lord Bardolph is here waiting for him.
PORTER. His lordship has gone out walking in the orchard. If you'll just knock at the gate, sir, he'll answer it himself.
[Enter Northumberland.]
LORD BARDOLPH. Here comes the Earl.
[Exit Porter.]

NORTHUMBERLAND. What news, Lord Bardolph? Every minute now ought to give birth to some new scheme. These are wild times. Conflict is like a horse stuffed with rich feed: it has broken loose in a frenzy and tramples everything in front of it.
LORD BARDOLPH. Noble earl, I bring you sure news from Shrewsbury.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Good, if God is willing!

LORD BARDOLPH. As good as any heart could wish. The King is wounded almost to death. Prince Harry has been killed outright, thanks to your son's good fortune. Both the Blunts were killed by Douglas. Young Prince John, Westmoreland and Stafford ran from the field. And Harry Monmouth's fat hulk, Sir John Falstaff, is your son's prisoner. Oh, such a day, so fought, so pursued and so handsomely won, has not come to honor our times since Caesar's victories!
NORTHUMBERLAND. How do you know all this? Did you see the battlefield? Did you come from Shrewsbury?
LORD BARDOLPH. I talked with a man who came from there, my lord. He was a well-bred gentleman with a good name, and he told me this news freely, as true.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Here comes my servant Travers, whom I sent last Tuesday to find out the news.
[Enter Travers.]
LORD BARDOLPH. My lord, I rode past him on the road. He has no certain news, apart from whatever he might perhaps pick up from me.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Now, Travers, what good news do you bring?

TRAVERS. My lord, Sir John Umfrevile turned me back with joyful news, and since his horse was better, he rode on ahead of me. After him came a gentleman spurring hard, nearly worn out with speed, who stopped beside me to let his bloodied horse catch its breath. He asked the way to Chester, and I asked him what news there was from Shrewsbury. He told me the rebellion had bad luck, and that young Harry Percy's spur was cold. With that he let his strong horse have its head, leaned forward and drove his armed heels into the panting sides of his poor nag, right up to the rowel. Then he shot off, looking as if he would devour the road, and he would not stay for any more questions.
NORTHUMBERLAND. What? Again: did he say young Harry Percy's spur was cold? Hotspur, Coldspur? That the rebellion had met bad luck?
LORD BARDOLPH. My lord, I'll tell you what. If your young son has not won the day, then on my honor, I'll give up my barony for a silk lace. Never speak of it again.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Then why would the gentleman who rode past Travers give such evidence of defeat?
LORD BARDOLPH. Who, him? He was some worthless fellow who had stolen the horse he rode, and on my life he was talking at random. Look, here comes more news.
[Enter Morton.]

NORTHUMBERLAND. Yes, this man's face is like the title page of a book: it announces the nature of a tragic volume. So looks the shore where the mighty flood has left proof of its invasion. Say, Morton, did you come from Shrewsbury?
MORTON. I ran from Shrewsbury, my noble lord, where hateful death put on his ugliest mask to terrify our side.

NORTHUMBERLAND. How are my son and my brother? You are trembling, and the whiteness of your cheeks tells your errand better than your tongue can. A man just like this, so faint, so lifeless, so dull, so dreadful to look at, so full of woe, once drew back Priam's curtain in the dead of night to tell him half of Troy was burned. But Priam saw the fire before he heard a word, and I have seen my Percy's death before you could report it. This is what you would say: "Your son did this and this. Your brother did that. Noble Douglas fought like so." You would stop my greedy ear with their bold deeds. But in the end, to stop my ear for good, you have a sigh to blow that praise away, ending with "Brother, son and all are dead."
MORTON. Douglas is alive, and so is your brother. But as for my lord your son—

NORTHUMBERLAND. Why, he is dead. See how quick a tongue suspicion has! A man who only fears the thing he does not want to know can read in other people's eyes, by instinct, that what he feared has happened. Still, speak, Morton. Tell an earl that his guess is a lie, and I will take it as a sweet insult and make you rich for wronging me like that.
MORTON. You are too great for me to contradict. Your instinct is too true and your fears too certain.

NORTHUMBERLAND. Even so, do not say that Percy is dead. I see a strange confession in your eye. You shake your head and think it a fear or a sin to speak the truth. If he is slain, say so. The tongue that reports a man's death does no wrong. The one who sins is the one who lies about the dead, not the one who says a dead man is not alive. Still, the first person to bring unwelcome news has a losing job, and his voice sounds forever after like a gloomy bell, remembered tolling for a friend who has departed.
LORD BARDOLPH. I cannot believe, my lord, that your son is dead.

MORTON. I am sorry to force you to believe what I wish to God I had not seen. But with these eyes I saw him, bloody, weary and out of breath, returning feeble blows to Harry Monmouth. Monmouth's swift fury beat the never-daunted Percy down to the ground, and he never rose from there alive. In short, his death, whose spirit lent fire even to the dullest peasant in his camp, took fire and heat away from the best-tempered courage in his troops as soon as it was spread about. His side had been steeled by his metal, and once that failed in him, all the rest turned on themselves, like dull, heavy lead. And as a heavy thing, when it is forced, flies with the greatest speed, so our men, weighed down by the loss of Hotspur, lent this weight such lightness with their fear. Arrows did not fly faster toward their target than our soldiers, aiming at their own safety, fled from the field. Then the noble Worcester was taken prisoner, too soon. And that furious Scot, the bloody Douglas, whose hard-working sword had three times killed someone who looked like the King, began to lower his pride. He gave cover to the shame of those who turned their backs, and in his flight, stumbling in fear, he was caught. The sum of it all is that the King has won, and has sent out a swift force to meet you, my lord, under the command of young Lancaster and Westmoreland. That is the news in full.

NORTHUMBERLAND. I will have time enough to mourn for this. There is medicine in poison. This news, which would have made me sick if I had been well, has in some measure made me well now that I am sick. Think of a wretch whose fever-weakened joints buckle under the weight of life like hinges with no strength. Impatient with his fit, he breaks out of his keeper's arms like a fire. In just that way my limbs, weakened by grief and now enraged by grief, are three times themselves. Away, then, you fussy crutch! A scaly gauntlet with steel joints must now glove this hand. And away, you sickly cap! You are too frail a guard for a head that princes, flushed with conquest, aim to hit. Now bind my brows with iron, and let the roughest hour that time and spite dare bring come to frown on enraged Northumberland! Let heaven kiss earth! Now let Nature's hand no longer hold back the wild flood! Let order die! Let this world no longer be a stage that feeds conflict in a long, drawn-out act. Let one spirit, that of Cain, the first-born, rule in every heart, so that with every heart set on bloody courses, the rough play may end, and darkness may be the burier of the dead!
LORD BARDOLPH. This strained passion wrongs you, my lord.

MORTON. Sweet earl, do not divorce wisdom from your honor. The lives of all your loving partners depend on your health, and if you give it up to stormy passion, they must fail. You weighed the outcome of war, my noble lord, and added up the account of chance, before you said "Let us raise an army." You foresaw that in the sharing out of blows your son might fall. You knew he walked over dangers, along an edge where he was more likely to fall in than get across. You were warned that his flesh could take wounds and scars, and that his eager spirit would lift him to wherever the most dangerous business was going on. Yet you said "Go forth." And none of this, though you felt it strongly, could hold back the stubbornly pursued undertaking. What has happened, then, or what has this bold enterprise produced, other than what was likely to happen?

LORD BARDOLPH. All of us who are involved in this loss knew we were venturing onto such dangerous seas that if we came through alive, it was ten to one. And yet we ventured, because the gain we were after choked out any thought of the likely danger we feared. Now that we are capsized, we will venture again. Come, we will put out to sea again, with body and goods.

MORTON. It is more than time. And, my most noble lord, I hear for certain, and dare to tell the truth: the gentle Archbishop of York is up in arms with a well-equipped force. He is a man who binds his followers with a double guarantee. My lord your son had only the corpse of an army to fight with, only shadows and shows of men. For that very word, "rebellion," split the action of their bodies from their souls. They fought queasily and under compulsion, like men drinking medicine, so that their weapons only seemed to be on our side. As for their spirits and souls, that word "rebellion" froze them up, as fish are frozen in a pond. But now the bishop turns insurrection into religion. He is thought sincere and holy in his thoughts, so he is followed with both body and mind. He swells his uprising with the blood of fair King Richard, scraped from the stones of Pomfret. He draws his quarrel and his cause from heaven. He tells them he stands astride a bleeding land, gasping for life under great Bolingbroke. And people of high and low rank flock to follow him.

NORTHUMBERLAND. I knew of this before. But to tell the truth, my present grief had wiped it from my mind. Come in with me, and advise every man on the best way to safety and revenge. Get messengers and letters, and make friends quickly. There were never so few of us, and never more need.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — London. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Falstaff, with his Page carrying his sword and shield.]
FALSTAFF. Boy, you giant, what did the doctor say about my urine?
PAGE. He said, sir, that the water itself was good, healthy water. But the man who produced it might have more diseases than he knew about.

FALSTAFF. Men of every sort take pride in jeering at me. The brain of this foolishly made lump of clay we call man cannot come up with anything funnier than what I invent, or what gets invented about me. I'm not only witty myself, I'm the reason other men are witty. Here I walk in front of you like a sow that has crushed all her litter but one. If the Prince gave you to me for any reason except to make me look good, then I have no judgment. You whoreson mandrake root, you're fitter to be worn in my cap than to wait at my heels. I've never had a servant as tiny as an agate stone on a ring until now. But I won't set you in gold or silver. I'll set you in shabby clothes and send you back to your master as a jewel: the youngster, the Prince your master, whose chin has no feathers yet. I'd sooner grow a beard in the palm of my hand than let him get one off his cheek. And still he won't hesitate to say his face is a face fit for a king. God can finish it when He likes, but there's not a hair out of place yet. He can go on calling it a royal face, because no barber will ever earn sixpence from it. And yet he's been crowing as if he'd been a grown man since his father was a bachelor. He may keep his own grace, but he's almost out of mine, I can tell him. What did Master Dommelton say about the satin for my short cloak and my breeches?
PAGE. He said, sir, that you should get him better security than Bardolph. He wouldn't take Bardolph's bond and yours. He didn't like the security.

FALSTAFF. Let him be damned like the glutton in the parable! I pray God his tongue is hotter! A whoreson Achitophel! A rascally yes-indeed knave, stringing a gentleman along and then insisting on security! These smooth-headed whoresons wear nothing now but high shoes and bunches of keys at their belts. And if a man deals with them in an honest purchase on credit, they insist on security. I'd as soon they put rat poison in my mouth as offer to stop it with security. I expected him to send me twenty-two yards of satin, as I'm a true knight, and he sends me "security." Well, he may sleep in security, for he has the horn of plenty, and the lightness of his wife shines through it. And yet he can't see, though he has his own lantern to light him. Where's Bardolph?
PAGE. He's gone to Smithfield to buy your worship a horse.
FALSTAFF. I bought him in Paul's, and he'll buy me a horse in Smithfield. If I could just get a wife in the brothels, I'd be supplied with a man, a horse and a wife.
[Enter the Lord Chief Justice and Servant.]
PAGE. Sir, here comes the nobleman who sent the Prince to prison for hitting him, over Bardolph.
FALSTAFF. Stay close by me. I won't see him.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Who's that going by?
SERVANT. Falstaff, if it please your lordship.
CHIEF JUSTICE. The one who was under investigation for the robbery?
SERVANT. The same, my lord. But he has done good service at Shrewsbury since then, and I hear he is now going with some command to Lord John of Lancaster.
CHIEF JUSTICE. What, to York? Call him back.
SERVANT. Sir John Falstaff!
FALSTAFF. Boy, tell him I'm deaf.
PAGE. You'll have to speak louder, my master is deaf.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I'm sure he is, when it comes to hearing anything good. Go and pull him by the elbow. I must speak with him.
SERVANT. Sir John!

FALSTAFF. What! A young rascal, and begging! Isn't there a war? Isn't there work to be had? Doesn't the King lack subjects? Don't the rebels need soldiers? It's a shame to be on any side but one. But it's a worse shame to beg than to be on the worst side, even if it were worse than the word "rebellion" can make it.
SERVANT. You misunderstand me, sir.
FALSTAFF. Why, sir, did I say you were an honest man? Setting my knighthood and my soldiership aside, I would have lied in my throat if I had said so.
SERVANT. Then I beg you, sir, set your knighthood and your soldiership aside, and give me leave to tell you that you lie in your throat if you say I am anything other than an honest man.

FALSTAFF. I give you leave to tell me that? I set aside what grows on me? If you get any leave from me, hang me. If you take leave, you'd better be hanged. You're following a false trail, like a hound running backward. Away! Get out!
SERVANT. Sir, my lord wants to speak with you.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Sir John Falstaff, a word with you.

FALSTAFF. My good lord! God give your lordship a good day. I'm glad to see your lordship out and about. I heard your lordship was sick. I hope your lordship is going out on a doctor's advice. Your lordship, though not completely past youth, still has a taste of age about you, a flavor of the saltiness of time. So I most humbly beg your lordship to take respectful care of your health.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Sir John, I sent for you before your expedition to Shrewsbury.
FALSTAFF. If it please your lordship, I hear his Majesty has come back from Wales in some distress.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I'm not talking about his Majesty. You wouldn't come when I sent for you.
FALSTAFF. And I hear, what's more, that his Highness has fallen into this same whoreson apoplexy.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Well, God cure him! Now please let me speak with you.
FALSTAFF. This apoplexy, as I understand it, is a kind of lethargy, if it please your lordship: a kind of sleeping in the blood, a whoreson tingling.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Why are you telling me about it? Let it be what it is.
FALSTAFF. It originates in much grief, in study, and in disturbance of the brain. I have read the cause of its effects in Galen. It's a kind of deafness.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I think you have caught the disease yourself, because you don't hear what I say to you.
FALSTAFF. Very well, my lord, very well. Rather, if it please you, it's the disease of not listening, the sickness of not paying attention, that troubles me.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Locking you up by the heels would improve the attention of your ears, and I wouldn't mind becoming your physician.

FALSTAFF. I'm as poor as Job, my lord, but not so patient. Your lordship may give me the medicine of imprisonment because of my poverty. But as for how I could be your patient and follow your prescriptions, the wise may make some tiny doubt of it, or indeed a full-sized doubt.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I sent for you to come and speak with me when there were charges against you that put your life at risk.
FALSTAFF. As my learned counsel in the laws of this land-service advised me at the time, I did not come.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Well, the truth is, Sir John, you live in great disgrace.
FALSTAFF. A man who buckles himself into my belt can't live in less.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Your means are very slender, and your waste is great.
FALSTAFF. I wish it were the other way around. I wish my means were greater and my waist slenderer.
CHIEF JUSTICE. You have led the young prince astray.
FALSTAFF. The young prince has led me astray. I'm the fellow with the great belly, and he's my dog.

CHIEF JUSTICE. Well, I'm reluctant to rub a newly healed wound. Your day's service at Shrewsbury has gilded over your night's exploit at Gad's Hill a little. You can thank the unquiet times for the quiet way that business was hurried past.
FALSTAFF. My lord!
CHIEF JUSTICE. But since all is well, keep it that way. Don't wake a sleeping wolf.
FALSTAFF. Waking a wolf is as bad as smelling a fox.
CHIEF JUSTICE. What! You're like a candle with the better part burnt out.
FALSTAFF. A revel candle, my lord, all tallow. If I said it was wax, my growth would bear out the truth.
CHIEF JUSTICE. There's not a white hair on your face that shouldn't have its effect of gravity.
FALSTAFF. Its effect of gravy, gravy, gravy.
CHIEF JUSTICE. You follow the young prince up and down like his evil angel.

FALSTAFF. Not so, my lord. Your evil angel is light, a coin that's underweight. But I hope the man who looks at me will take me without weighing me. And yet in some respects, I admit, I can't pass as good coin. I can't say. Virtue is so little regarded in these fruit-peddlers' times that true courage has been turned into a bear-keeper. Quick intelligence has been made a barman, and has its sharp wit wasted on adding up bills. All the other gifts that belong to a man, as the malice of this age shapes them, are not worth a gooseberry. You who are old don't consider the capacities of us who are young. You measure the heat of our livers by the bitterness of your own gall. And those of us in the vanguard of our youth, I must confess, are wags too.

CHIEF JUSTICE. Do you write your name in the scroll of youth, when you are written down as old in every feature of age? Don't you have a watery eye, a dry hand, a yellow cheek, a white beard, a shrinking leg and a swelling belly? Isn't your voice cracked, your breath short, your chin double, your wit single, and every part of you blasted with age? And will you still call yourself young? Shame, shame, shame, Sir John!

FALSTAFF. My lord, I was born around three o'clock in the afternoon, with a white head and a somewhat round belly. As for my voice, I lost it hollering and singing hymns. I won't offer any more proof of my youth. The truth is, I'm only old in judgment and understanding. And any man who wants to caper with me for a thousand marks, let him lend me the money, and I'll go at him! As for the box on the ear the Prince gave you, he gave it like a rough prince, and you took it like a sensible lord. I've scolded him for it, and the young lion is sorry. Indeed, not in ashes and sackcloth, but in new silk and old sack.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Well, God send the Prince a better companion!
FALSTAFF. God send the companion a better prince! I can't get him off my hands.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Well, the King has separated you and Prince Harry. I hear you are going with Lord John of Lancaster against the Archbishop and the Earl of Northumberland.

FALSTAFF. Yes, and I thank your pretty sweet wit for that. But mind you pray, all of you who kiss my lady Peace at home, that our armies don't meet on a hot day. By the Lord, I'm taking only two shirts with me, and I don't mean to sweat extraordinarily. If it's a hot day and I wave anything but a bottle, I hope I never spit white again. There's no dangerous action that can stick its head out but I get shoved into it. Well, I can't last forever. But it has always been the way of us English, when we have a good thing, to make it too common. If you insist on calling me an old man, you ought to give me rest. I wish to God my name weren't as terrible to the enemy as it is. I'd rather be eaten to death by rust than be scoured away to nothing by constant motion.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Well, be honest, be honest, and God bless your expedition!
FALSTAFF. Will your lordship lend me a thousand pounds to fit me out?
CHIEF JUSTICE. Not a penny, not a penny. You're too impatient to bear crosses, whether coins or troubles. Farewell. Give my regards to my cousin Westmoreland.
[Exeunt Chief Justice and Servant.]

FALSTAFF. If I do, flick me with a three-man mallet. A man can no more separate old age from greed than he can separate young limbs from lechery. But the gout torments the one, and the pox pinches the other, so both ages cut off my curses before I can use them. Boy!
PAGE. Sir?
FALSTAFF. What money is in my purse?
PAGE. Seven groats and two pence.

FALSTAFF. I can find no cure for this wasting sickness of the purse. Borrowing only drags it out and drags it out, but the disease is incurable. Go, take this letter to my Lord of Lancaster, this one to the Prince, this one to the Earl of Westmoreland, and this one to old Mistress Ursula, whom I have sworn every week to marry since I noticed the first white hair on my chin. Get to it. You know where to find me. [_Exit Page_.] A pox on this gout! Or a gout on this pox! One or the other is playing the rogue with my big toe. It doesn't matter if I limp. I have the wars as my excuse, and my pension will seem all the more reasonable. A good wit makes use of anything. I will turn diseases to profit.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — York. The Archbishop’s palace
paragraphs: [Enter the Archbishop, the Lords Hastings, Mowbray and Bardolph.]
ARCHBISHOP. So now you have heard our cause and learned what forces we have. My most noble friends, I ask you all to say plainly what you think of our hopes. And first, Lord Marshal, what do you say?

MOWBRAY. I fully accept the reason for our taking up arms. But I would gladly be better satisfied about how, with the forces we have, we can advance ourselves boldly enough to face the power and might of the King.

HASTINGS. Our muster rolls now add up to twenty-five thousand picked men. And our reinforcements depend heavily on the hope of great Northumberland, whose heart burns with a furious fire over the wrongs done to him.
LORD BARDOLPH. Then the question stands like this, Lord Hastings: can our present twenty-five thousand hold their heads up without Northumberland?
HASTINGS. With him, we can.

LORD BARDOLPH. Yes, indeed, that's the point. But if we are thought too weak without him, my judgment is that we should not go too far until we have his help in hand. In a business as bloody as this, guesses, expectations and hunches about uncertain help should not be admitted.
ARCHBISHOP. That is very true, Lord Bardolph, for that was exactly young Hotspur's case at Shrewsbury.

LORD BARDOLPH. It was, my lord. He padded himself with hope, living on air on the promise of reinforcements. He flattered himself with plans for an army much smaller than the smallest of his thoughts. And so, with the great imagination that belongs to madmen, he led his forces to death and leapt blindfolded into destruction.
HASTINGS. But with your permission, it has never yet done harm to set out likelihoods and shapes of hope.

LORD BARDOLPH. Yes, it does, if the present nature of war, the immediate action, a cause that's already under way, lives on hope the way we see buds appearing in early spring. Hope gives less assurance that those buds will bear fruit than despair gives that frost will bite them. When we mean to build, we first survey the site, then draw the plan. When we see the shape of the house, we must estimate the cost of putting it up. And if we find that cost outweighs our means, what do we do but draw the plan again with fewer rooms, or at least give up building altogether? Much more, in this great work, which is almost to pull down a kingdom and set up another, we should survey the site and the plan. We should agree on a sure foundation, question the surveyors, and know our own estate: how able it is to undertake such a work and weigh against our opponent. Otherwise we fortify on paper and in figures, using the names of men instead of men. We would be like someone who draws the plan of a house beyond his power to build, who gives up halfway and leaves his half-made expense as a naked target for the weeping clouds and a ruin for harsh winter's tyranny.

HASTINGS. Suppose our hopes, though they were born likely to live, should be stillborn, and suppose we now had in hand every last man we expected. I think we are still a body strong enough, just as we are, to match the King.
LORD BARDOLPH. What, is the King's army only twenty-five thousand?

HASTINGS. Against us, no more. No, not even that many, Lord Bardolph. As the times brawl, his forces are split into three heads: one army against the French, one against Glendower, and a third by necessity must take us on. So the unsteady king is divided in three, and his treasury rings hollow with poverty and emptiness.
ARCHBISHOP. There's no need to fear that he will draw his separate forces together and come against us in full strength.
HASTINGS. If he did, he would leave his back unarmed, with the French and the Welsh baying at his heels. Never fear that.
LORD BARDOLPH. Who is likely to lead his forces here?
HASTINGS. The Duke of Lancaster and Westmoreland. Against the Welsh, the King himself and Harry Monmouth. But who has been put in place against the French, I have no certain information.

ARCHBISHOP. Let us go on and make public the reason for our taking up arms. The commonwealth is sick of its own choice. Its overgreedy love has made it gorge itself. A man who builds on the heart of the common people has a giddy and unsafe home. Oh you foolish multitude, with what loud applause you beat heaven with blessings on Bolingbroke, before he was what you wanted him to be! And now that he is dressed in your own desires, you beastly feeder, you are so full of him that you provoke yourself to throw him up. Just so, you common dog, you disgorged royal Richard from your glutton's belly. And now you would eat your dead vomit up again, and howl because you can't find it. What trust can there be in these times? Those who wanted Richard dead while he lived have now fallen in love with his grave. You who threw dust on his goodly head when he came sighing through proud London behind the admired heels of Bolingbroke now cry "Oh earth, give us that king back, and take this one!" Oh, the thoughts of men are accursed! The past and the future seem best. The present is always worst.
MOWBRAY. Shall we go and gather our numbers, and set out?
HASTINGS. We are time's subjects, and time tells us to go.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — London. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Hostess with two Officers, Fang and Snare, following.]
HOSTESS. Master Fang, have you filed the case?
FANG. It's filed.
HOSTESS. Where's your assistant? Is he a strong fellow? Will he hold up?
FANG. Hey, where's Snare?
HOSTESS. Oh Lord, yes! Good Master Snare.
SNARE. Here, here.
FANG. Snare, we have to arrest Sir John Falstaff.
HOSTESS. Yes, good Master Snare, I've put his name down and everything.
SNARE. It might cost some of us our lives, because he'll stab.

HOSTESS. Oh, heaven help us, watch out for him. He stabbed me in my own house, and in the most beastly way, honestly. He doesn't care what harm he does once his sword is out. He'll thrust like a devil. He won't spare man, woman or child.
FANG. If I can grapple with him, I don't care about his thrusts.
HOSTESS. No, and neither do I. I'll be right at your elbow.
FANG. If I can only get a fist on him once, if he just comes within my grip —

HOSTESS. His going away will ruin me, I promise you. He's an infinitive amount on my tab. Good Master Fang, hold him tight. Good Master Snare, don't let him get away. He's always coming to Pie Corner — begging your pardon, gentlemen — to buy a saddle. And he's invited to dinner at the Lubber's Head in Lumbert Street, at Master Smooth the silk merchant's. Please, since my action is filed and my case is so publicly known, have him brought in to answer for it. A hundred marks is a heavy load for a poor woman on her own to carry. I have carried it, and carried it, and carried it, and I've been fobbed off, and fobbed off, and fobbed off, from this day to that day, until it's a shame even to think about. There's no honesty in dealing like that, unless a woman is supposed to be made an ass and a beast, to put up with every rogue's wrong. Here he comes, and that downright wine-red-nosed rogue Bardolph is with him. Do your duty, do your duty, Master Fang and Master Snare. Do me, do me, do me your duty.
[Enter Falstaff, Bardolph and Page.]
FALSTAFF. What's this, whose mare is dead? What's the matter?
FANG. Sir John, I arrest you at the suit of Mistress Quickly.
FALSTAFF. Get away, you scoundrels! Draw your sword, Bardolph! Cut the villain's head off. Throw the slut in the gutter.

HOSTESS. Throw me in the gutter? I'll throw you in the gutter. Will you, will you, you bastard rogue? Murder, murder! Oh, you honeysuckle villain, will you kill God's officers and the King's? Oh, you honeyseed rogue, you're a honeyseed, a man-killer and a woman-killer.
FALSTAFF. Keep them off, Bardolph.
FANG. A rescue! A rescue!
HOSTESS. Good people, bring a rescue or two. You will, will you? You will, will you? Go on, go on, you rogue! Go on, you gallows-bird!
PAGE. Get away, you scullion! You rampallian! You fustilarian! I'll tickle your catastrophe.
[Enter the Lord Chief Justice and his men.]
CHIEF JUSTICE. What's the matter? Keep the peace here, you!
HOSTESS. My good lord, be good to me. Please, stand by me.

CHIEF JUSTICE. What is this, Sir John? Why are you brawling here? Is this fitting for your rank, the time, and your business? You should be well on your way to York by now. Stand away from him, fellow. Why are you hanging on him?
HOSTESS. Oh, my most worshipful lord, if it please your Grace, I'm a poor widow of Eastcheap, and he's being arrested on my suit.
CHIEF JUSTICE. For what sum?

HOSTESS. It's more than a sum, my lord. It's everything, everything I have. He has eaten me out of house and home. He has put all I own into that fat belly of his. But I'll get some of it back out, or I'll ride you at night like the nightmare.
FALSTAFF. I think I'd be just as likely to ride the mare, if I had some higher ground to climb up from.

CHIEF JUSTICE. How did this come about, Sir John? Shame on you! What man of decent temper would put up with this storm of shouting? Aren't you ashamed to force a poor widow to such rough measures just to get what's hers?
FALSTAFF. What's the total I owe you?

HOSTESS. Why, if you were an honest man, yourself and the money too. You swore to me on a partly gilded goblet, sitting in my Dolphin room, at the round table, by a coal fire, on Wednesday in Whitsun week, when the Prince broke your head for comparing his father to a singing-man of Windsor. You swore to me then, while I was washing your wound, that you would marry me and make me your lady wife. Can you deny it? Didn't Goodwife Keech, the butcher's wife, come in just then and call me neighbor Quickly? She came in to borrow a bowl of vinegar and told us she had a good dish of prawns, and you wanted some, and I told you they were bad for a fresh wound. And when she'd gone downstairs, didn't you ask me not to be so familiar with such poor people, saying that before long they'd call me madam? And didn't you kiss me and tell me to fetch you thirty shillings? I put you now to your oath on the Bible. Deny it, if you can.

FALSTAFF. My lord, this is a poor mad soul. She says all over town that her eldest son looks like you. She used to be well off, and the truth is that poverty has driven her out of her mind. But as for these foolish officers, I beg you to let me have redress against them.

CHIEF JUSTICE. Sir John, Sir John, I know well how you twist a true case the wrong way. A bold face won't do it, and neither will the flood of words that comes with such worse-than-shameless cheek from you. None of it can push me away from a fair judgment. It seems to me that you have worked on this woman's easily yielding nature and made her serve your needs, both with her purse and with her person.
HOSTESS. Yes, truly, my lord.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Please, be quiet. Pay her the debt you owe her, and undo the wrong you've done her. You can do the one with sterling money and the other with prompt repentance.

FALSTAFF. My lord, I won't take this snub without answering. You call honorable boldness shameless cheek. If a man bows and says nothing, he's virtuous. No, my lord, with all due respect, I won't be your petitioner. I tell you, I want to be freed from these officers, since I'm on urgent business for the King.
CHIEF JUSTICE. You talk as if you had the power to do wrong. But answer in a way that fits your reputation, and satisfy the poor woman.
FALSTAFF. Come here, hostess.
[Enter Gower.]
CHIEF JUSTICE. Now, Master Gower, what news?
GOWER. The King, my lord, and Harry, Prince of Wales, are close at hand. The paper tells the rest.
FALSTAFF. On my word as a gentleman.
HOSTESS. Indeed, you said that before.
FALSTAFF. On my word as a gentleman. Come, no more talk about it.
HOSTESS. By this heavenly ground I'm standing on, I'll have to pawn both my silver and the tapestries in my dining rooms.

FALSTAFF. Glasses, glasses, are the only way to drink. And for your walls, a nice light painted joke, or the story of the Prodigal Son, or the German hunt in watercolor, is worth a thousand of these bed-hangings and these fly-bitten tapestries. Make it ten pounds, if you can. Come, if it weren't for your moods, there isn't a better woman in England. Go, wash your face, and drop the case. Come, you mustn't be in this mood with me. Don't you know me? Come, come, I know you were put up to this.
HOSTESS. Please, Sir John, make it only twenty nobles. Truly, I hate to pawn my silver, so help me God!
FALSTAFF. Forget it, I'll find another way. You'll always be a fool.
HOSTESS. Well, you shall have it, even if I pawn my gown. I hope you'll come to supper. You'll pay me everything together?
FALSTAFF. As surely as I live! [_To Bardolph_.] Go with her, with her. Stick close, stick close.
HOSTESS. Will you have Doll Tearsheet meet you at supper?
FALSTAFF. No more talk, let's have her.
[Exeunt Hostess, Fang, Snare, Bardolph and Page.]
CHIEF JUSTICE. I have heard better news.
FALSTAFF. What's the news, my lord?
CHIEF JUSTICE. Where did the King spend last night?
GOWER. At Basingstoke, my lord.
FALSTAFF. I hope, my lord, that all's well. What is the news, my lord?
CHIEF JUSTICE. Are all his forces coming back?
GOWER. No. Fifteen hundred foot soldiers and five hundred cavalry have marched up to my Lord of Lancaster, against Northumberland and the Archbishop.
FALSTAFF. Is the King coming back from Wales, my noble lord?
CHIEF JUSTICE. You'll have letters from me shortly. Come along with me, good Master Gower.
FALSTAFF. My lord!
CHIEF JUSTICE. What is it?
FALSTAFF. Master Gower, may I ask you to dine with me?
GOWER. I must attend my good lord here. Thank you, good Sir John.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Sir John, you're dawdling here too long, since you're supposed to recruit soldiers in the counties as you go.
FALSTAFF. Will you have supper with me, Master Gower?
CHIEF JUSTICE. What foolish master taught you these manners, Sir John?
FALSTAFF. Master Gower, if they don't suit me, he was a fool who taught them to me. This is the proper fencing style, my lord: blow for blow, and then part on fair terms.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Now the Lord enlighten you, you are a great fool.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — London. Another street
paragraphs: [Enter Prince Henry and Poins.]
PRINCE HENRY. By God, I'm extremely tired.
POINS. Has it come to that? I thought weariness wouldn't dare touch someone of such high blood.
PRINCE HENRY. It does, though it spoils the color of my greatness to admit it. Isn't it shameful of me to want small beer?
POINS. Well, a prince shouldn't be so careless in his tastes as to remember such a weak drink.

PRINCE HENRY. Then my appetite probably wasn't princely in its making, because I really do remember the poor creature small beer. But these humble thoughts make me sick of my own greatness. What a disgrace it is for me to remember your name! Or to know your face tomorrow! Or to notice how many pairs of silk stockings you own — these, and the peach-colored ones you used to have! Or to keep a list of your shirts, one spare and another for use! But the tennis-court keeper knows that better than I do. It's a low ebb of linen with you when you aren't playing racket there, as you haven't for a good while, because the rest of your low countries have managed to eat up your Holland cloth. And God knows whether the ones who squall out of the ruins of your linen will inherit his kingdom. But the midwives say the children aren't to blame. That's how the world grows, and families get mightily strengthened.
POINS. How badly it fits that after working so hard you should talk so idly! Tell me, how many good young princes would do this, with their fathers as sick as yours is right now?
PRINCE HENRY. Shall I tell you one thing, Poins?
POINS. Yes, and make it an excellent thing.
PRINCE HENRY. It will do for wits of no higher breeding than yours.
POINS. Go on, I'll stand up to the thrust of this one thing you're going to tell.

PRINCE HENRY. Well, I tell you it isn't right for me to be sad now that my father is sick. Though I could tell you, as someone I choose, for lack of a better, to call my friend, that I could be sad, and sad indeed.
POINS. Hardly, on such a subject.

PRINCE HENRY. By this hand, you think I'm as deep in the devil's book as you and Falstaff are for hardness and stubbornness. Let the end prove the man. But I tell you, my heart bleeds inwardly that my father is so sick. And keeping such vile company as you has, naturally, taken from me any show of sorrow.
POINS. The reason?
PRINCE HENRY. What would you think of me if I wept?
POINS. I would think you a most princely hypocrite.

PRINCE HENRY. That would be everyone's thought, and you're a blessed fellow to think what everyone thinks. No man's thought in the world keeps to the main road better than yours. Everyone would indeed think me a hypocrite. And what prompts your most worshipful thought to think so?
POINS. Why, because you've been so wild and so grafted onto Falstaff.
PRINCE HENRY. And onto you.

POINS. By this light, I'm well spoken of. I can hear it with my own ears. The worst they can say of me is that I'm a second son and a good fellow with my hands. Those two things, I admit, I can't help. By the mass, here comes Bardolph.
[Enter Bardolph and Page.]
PRINCE HENRY. And the boy I gave Falstaff. He got him from me a Christian, and look whether the fat villain hasn't turned him into an ape.
BARDOLPH. God save your Grace!
PRINCE HENRY. And yours, most noble Bardolph!
POINS. Come on, you virtuous ass, you bashful fool, do you have to blush? Why are you blushing now? What a maidenly soldier you've become! Is it such a big matter to take a two-quart pot's virginity?

PAGE. He called me just now, my lord, through a red lattice window, and I couldn't make out any part of his face from there. At last I spotted his eyes, and I thought he had made two holes in the alewife's new petticoat and was peeping through them.
PRINCE HENRY. Hasn't the boy come along well?
BARDOLPH. Get away, you whoreson upright rabbit, get away!
PAGE. Get away, you rascally Althaea's dream, get away!
PRINCE HENRY. Explain it to us, boy. What dream, boy?
PAGE. Why, my lord, Althaea dreamed she gave birth to a burning torch, and so I call him her dream.
PRINCE HENRY. That's a crown's worth of good interpretation. There it is, boy.
POINS. Oh, if only this blossom could be kept from cankers! Well, here's sixpence to preserve you.
BARDOLPH. If you don't all see to it that he's hanged, the gallows will be cheated.
PRINCE HENRY. And how is your master, Bardolph?
BARDOLPH. Well, my lord. He heard that your Grace was coming to town. Here's a letter for you.
POINS. Delivered with great respect. And how is the Martinmas beef, your master?
BARDOLPH. In bodily health, sir.
POINS. Well, it's his immortal part that needs a doctor, but that doesn't bother him. Though it's sick, it doesn't die.
PRINCE HENRY. I let this wen be as familiar with me as my dog, and he keeps his place. Look how he writes.
POINS.
[_Reads_.] "John Falstaff, knight," Every man must know that, as often as

he has occasion to name himself. It's just like those who are related to the King. They never prick a finger without saying, "There's some of the King's blood spilled." "How does that come about?" says the man who pretends not to understand. The answer is as ready as a borrower's cap: "I am the King's poor cousin, sir."

PRINCE HENRY. No, they'll claim kinship with us, or else they'll fetch it from Japhet. But to the letter: "Sir John Falstaff, knight, to the son of the King, nearest his father, Harry, Prince of Wales, greeting."
POINS. Why, this is a certificate.
PRINCE HENRY. Quiet! "I will imitate the honorable Romans in brevity."
POINS. He surely means brevity of breath, short-winded.

PRINCE HENRY. "I commend myself to you, I commend you, and I leave you. Don't be too familiar with Poins, because he abuses your favors so much that he swears you are going to marry his sister Nell. Repent in your idle hours as you can, and so, farewell. Yours by yes and no, which is as much as to say, by the way you use him — Jack Falstaff with my familiars, John with my brothers and sisters, and Sir John with all Europe."
POINS. My lord, I'll soak this letter in sack and make him eat it.
PRINCE HENRY. That would make him eat twenty of his words. But do you treat me like this, Ned? Must I marry your sister?
POINS. God send the girl no worse luck! But I never said so.
PRINCE HENRY. Well, this is how we play the fool with time, while the spirits of the wise sit in the clouds and mock us. Is your master here in London?
BARDOLPH. Yes, my lord.
PRINCE HENRY. Where does he sup? Does the old boar feed in the old sty?
BARDOLPH. At the old place, my lord, in Eastcheap.
PRINCE HENRY. What company?
PAGE. Ephesians, my lord, of the old church.
PRINCE HENRY. Do any women sup with him?
PAGE. None, my lord, except old Mistress Quickly and Mistress Doll Tearsheet.
PRINCE HENRY. What pagan may that be?
PAGE. A proper gentlewoman, sir, and a kinswoman of my master's.
PRINCE HENRY. Kin in the way the parish heifers are kin to the town bull. Shall we sneak up on them at supper, Ned?
POINS. I am your shadow, my lord. I'll follow you.
PRINCE HENRY. You, boy, and Bardolph, not a word to your master that I've come to town. Here's something for your silence.
BARDOLPH. I have no tongue, sir.
PAGE. And as for mine, sir, I'll govern it.
PRINCE HENRY. Farewell. Go.
[Exeunt Bardolph and Page.]
This Doll Tearsheet must be some well-traveled road.
POINS. I assure you, she's as common as the road between Saint Albans and London.
PRINCE HENRY. How could we see Falstaff behave tonight in his true colors, without being seen ourselves?
POINS. Put on two leather jerkins and aprons, and wait on him at his table as drawers.

PRINCE HENRY. From a god to a bull? A heavy fall! That was Jove's case. From a prince to an apprentice? A low transformation, and it will be mine, because in everything the purpose must outweigh the folly. Follow me, Ned.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — Warkworth. Before the castle
paragraphs: [Enter Northumberland, Lady Northumberland and Lady Percy.]
NORTHUMBERLAND. I beg you, loving wife and gentle daughter, give way to my rough business. Don't put on the face of the times and be troublesome to Percy, as they are.
LADY NORTHUMBERLAND. I've given up. I won't speak anymore. Do what you will, and let your own wisdom guide you.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Alas, sweet wife, my honor is in pawn, and nothing but my going can redeem it.

LADY PERCY. Oh, for God's sake, please don't go to this war! There was a time, father, when you broke your word, when you were more bound to it than now. Your own Percy, my heart's dear Harry, kept looking north to see his father bring up his forces, and he looked in vain. Who persuaded you then to stay at home? Two honors were lost, yours and your son's. As for yours, may the God of heaven make it bright again! As for his, it clung to him like the sun in the gray vault of heaven, and by its light all the chivalry of England moved to brave deeds. He was truly the mirror in which noble young men dressed themselves. No man had legs that didn't practice his walk. And his thick speech, which nature made his flaw, became the accent of the brave. Even those who could speak low and slowly would ruin their own perfect speech to seem like him. So in speech, in walk, in diet, in what he loved, in military rules and moods of blood, he was the mark and mirror, the copy and book, that shaped others. And him — oh, wondrous him! Oh, miracle of men! — him you abandoned, second to none, but not seconded by you, to face the hideous god of war at a disadvantage, to hold a field where nothing but the sound of Hotspur's name seemed to offer defense. That's how you left him. Never, oh never, do his ghost the wrong of holding your honor more strictly and carefully for others than for him! Leave them alone. The Marshal and the Archbishop are strong. If my sweet Harry had had even half their numbers, today I might be hanging on Hotspur's neck and talking of Monmouth's grave.

NORTHUMBERLAND. Curse your heart, fair daughter! You drain my spirits from me by lamenting old mistakes all over again. But I must go and meet danger there, or it will seek me out in another place and find me worse prepared.
LADY NORTHUMBERLAND. Oh, flee to Scotland, until the nobles and the armed commons have made a little trial of their strength.

LADY PERCY. If they gain ground and the upper hand against the King, then join them like a rib of steel to make their strength stronger. But for the sake of all our love, let them try themselves first. So did your son. He was left to it. That's how I came to be a widow, and I will never live long enough to rain on his memory with my eyes, so that it grows and sprouts as high as heaven, a lasting record for my noble husband.

NORTHUMBERLAND. Come, come, go in with me. My mind is like the tide swelled up to its height, which stands still and runs neither way. I would gladly go to meet the Archbishop, but many thousand reasons hold me back. I'll resolve on Scotland. There I'll stay until time and opportunity ask for my company.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — London. The Boar’s head Tavern in Eastcheap
paragraphs: [Enter two Drawers.]
FIRST DRAWER. What the devil have you brought there — apple-johns? You know Sir John can't stand an apple-john.

SECOND DRAWER. By the mass, you're right. The Prince once set a dish of apple-johns in front of him and told him there were five more Sir Johns. Then he took off his hat and said, "I'll now take my leave of these six dry, round, old, withered knights." It angered him to the heart. But he's forgotten that.

FIRST DRAWER. Well then, cover them up and set them down, and see if you can find Sneak's band. Mistress Tearsheet would like to hear some music. Hurry. The room where they had supper is too hot, and they'll be coming in right away.
SECOND DRAWER. Listen, the Prince and Master Poins will be here soon, and they'll put on two of our jerkins and aprons. Sir John mustn't know about it. Bardolph brought word.
FIRST DRAWER. By the mass, there'll be a great old time. It will be an excellent trick.
SECOND DRAWER. I'll see if I can find Sneak.
[Exit.]
[Enter Hostess and Doll Tearsheet.]

HOSTESS. Truly, sweetheart, I think you're in an excellent good temperality now. Your pulsidge is beating as extraordinarily as a heart could want, and your color, I promise you, is as red as any rose, honestly! But really, you've drunk too much canary wine, and that's a wonderfully searching wine. It perfumes the blood before you can say "What's this?" How are you now?
DOLL. Better than I was. Hem!
HOSTESS. Well, that's good to hear. A good heart's worth gold. Look, here comes Sir John.
[Enter Falstaff.]
FALSTAFF.
[_Singing_.] "When Arthur first in court" — Empty the chamber pot.
[_Exit First Drawer_.] — [_Singing_.] "And was a worthy king."
Well now, Mistress Doll!
HOSTESS. Sick from a calm, yes, truly.
FALSTAFF. So is all her kind. Once they're in a calm, they're sick.
DOLL. A pox on you, you muddy rascal! Is that all the comfort you give me?
FALSTAFF. You make fat rascals, Mistress Doll.
DOLL. I make them? Gluttony and diseases make them. I don't.
FALSTAFF. If the cook helps make the gluttony, you help make the diseases, Doll. We catch them from you, Doll. We catch them from you. Grant me that, my poor virtue, grant me that.
DOLL. Yes, my joy, our chains and our jewels.

FALSTAFF. "Your brooches, pearls, and ornaments." For to serve bravely is to come off limping, you know. To come off the breach with your pike bravely bent, and to go to the surgeon bravely. To venture bravely on the loaded chambers —
DOLL. Go hang yourself, you muddy conger eel, hang yourself!

HOSTESS. Honestly, this is the same old story. You two never meet without falling into some quarrel. You're both, truly, as rheumatic as two dry toasts. Neither of you can put up with the other's confirmities. What in the world! One must give way, and that must be you. You're the weaker vessel, as they say, the emptier vessel.

DOLL. Can a weak empty vessel carry such a huge full barrel? There's a whole merchant's venture of Bordeaux wine in him. You've never seen a big ship better stuffed in the hold. Come, I'll be friends with you, Jack. You're going to the wars, and whether I'll ever see you again or not, nobody cares.
[Enter First Drawer.]
FIRST DRAWER. Sir, Ancient Pistol is downstairs and would like to speak with you.
DOLL. Hang him, the swaggering rascal! Don't let him come up here. He's the foulest-mouthed rogue in England.

HOSTESS. If he swaggers, don't let him come here. No, by my faith, I have to live among my neighbors. I'll have no swaggerers. My name and reputation stand good with the very best. Shut the door. No swaggerers come in here. I haven't lived all this while to have swaggering now. Shut the door, please.
FALSTAFF. Do you hear, hostess?
HOSTESS. Please calm yourself, Sir John. No swaggerers come in here.
FALSTAFF. Do you hear? It's my ensign.

HOSTESS. Nonsense, Sir John, don't tell me that. Our ensign, the swaggerer, doesn't come through my doors. I was before Master Tisick, the deputy, the other day, and as he said to me — it was no longer ago than last Wednesday, truly — "Neighbor Quickly," he says — Master Dumb, our minister, was there then — "Neighbor Quickly," he says, "receive those who are civil, because," he said, "you have a bad name." Now, I can tell why he said so. "Because," he says, "you are an honest woman and well thought of. So take care what guests you receive. Receive," he says, "no swaggering fellows." None come here. You'd bless yourself to hear what he said. No, I'll have no swaggerers.

FALSTAFF. He's no swaggerer, hostess. He's a tame cheat, truly. You can stroke him as gently as a greyhound puppy. He wouldn't swagger even with a Barbary hen, if her feathers ruffled up in any show of resistance. Call him up, drawer.
[Exit First Drawer.]

HOSTESS. A cheat, do you call him? I won't bar any honest man from my house, nor any cheat either. But I don't like swaggering, truly. I get worse whenever anyone says "swagger." Feel, gentlemen, how I shake. Look, I promise you.
DOLL. So you do, hostess.
HOSTESS. Do I? Yes, truly I do, like an aspen leaf. I can't stand swaggerers.
[Enter Pistol, Bardolph and Page.]
PISTOL. God save you, Sir John!
FALSTAFF. Welcome, Ancient Pistol. Here, Pistol, I load you with a cup of sack. Now fire off at my hostess.
PISTOL. I'll fire at her, Sir John, with two bullets.
FALSTAFF. She's pistol-proof, sir. You won't hurt her easily.
HOSTESS. Come, I'll drink no proofs and no bullets. I'll drink no more than does me good, not for any man's pleasure, not me.
PISTOL. Then to you, Mistress Dorothy! I will load you.
DOLL. Load me! I scorn you, you scurvy fellow. What, you poor, low, rascally, cheating, shirtless mate! Get away, you moldy rogue, get away! I'm meat for your master.
PISTOL. I know you, Mistress Dorothy.

DOLL. Get away, you cutpurse rascal, you filthy bung, get away! By this wine, I'll thrust my knife into your moldy jaws if you play the saucy cutthroat with me. Get away, you bottle-ale rascal, you stale basket-hilted juggler! Since when, I ask you, sir? God's light, with two ribbons on your shoulder? Some nerve!
PISTOL. May God not let me live, but I will murder your ruff for this.
FALSTAFF. No more, Pistol! I won't have you go off here. Discharge yourself from our company, Pistol.
HOSTESS. No, good Captain Pistol, not here, sweet captain.

DOLL. Captain! You abominable damned cheat, aren't you ashamed to be called captain? If captains agreed with me, they'd beat you out with clubs for taking their title before you've earned it. You a captain? You slave, for what? For tearing a poor whore's ruff in a brothel? He, a captain! Hang him, rogue. He lives on moldy stewed prunes and dried cakes. A captain? God's light, these villains will make the word as hateful as the word "occupy," which was an excellent good word before it was put to bad company. So captains had better look out.
BARDOLPH. Please go downstairs, good ensign.
FALSTAFF. Listen here, Mistress Doll.
PISTOL. Not I. I'll tell you what, Corporal Bardolph, I could tear her apart. I'll have revenge on her.
PAGE. Please go downstairs.

PISTOL. I'll see her damned first, down to Pluto's damned lake, by this hand, to the infernal deep, with Erebus and vile tortures too. Hold hook and line, I say. Down, down, dogs! Down, cheats! Don't we have Hiren here?
HOSTESS. Good Captain Peesel, be quiet. It's very late, truly. I beseech you now, aggravate your anger.

PISTOL. These are good humors, indeed! Shall pack-horses and hollow, pampered nags of Asia, who can't go more than thirty miles a day, compare with Caesars and with Cannibals and Trojan Greeks? No, rather damn them with King Cerberus, and let the sky roar. Shall we quarrel over trifles?
HOSTESS. Truly, captain, these are very bitter words.
BARDOLPH. Be gone, good ensign. This will turn into a brawl soon.
PISTOL. Do men die like dogs? Do they give crowns like pins? Don't we have Hiren here?
HOSTESS. On my word, captain, there's nobody like that here. What in the world, do you think I would deny her? For God's sake, be quiet.

PISTOL. Then feed and be fat, my fair Calipolis. Come, give us some sack. _Si fortune me tormente, sperato me contento._ Do we fear broadsides? No, let the fiend fire. Give me some sack. And, sweetheart, lie there.
[Laying down his sword.]
Do we come to full stops here? And are etceteras nothing?
FALSTAFF. Pistol, I would be quiet.
PISTOL. Sweet knight, I kiss your fist. What! We have seen the seven stars.
DOLL. For God's sake, throw him downstairs. I can't stand such a bombastic rascal.
PISTOL. Throw him downstairs? Don't we know Galloway nags?
FALSTAFF. Toss him down, Bardolph, like a shove-groat shilling. If he does nothing but talk nothing, he'll be nothing here.
BARDOLPH. Come, get downstairs.
PISTOL. What! Shall we have cutting? Shall we draw blood?
[Snatching up his sword.]
Then let death rock me asleep and cut short my sorrowful days! Why then, let grievous, ghastly, gaping wounds unwind the Three Sisters of Fate! Come, Atropos, I say!
HOSTESS. Here's fine stuff coming!
FALSTAFF. Give me my rapier, boy.
DOLL. Please, Jack, please, don't draw your sword.
FALSTAFF. Get downstairs.
[Drawing, and driving Pistol out.]
HOSTESS. What a commotion! I'll swear off keeping a tavern before I'll live in this fear and uproar. It's murder, I'll bet, for sure. Oh no, oh no, put away your bare weapons, put them away.
[Exeunt Bardolph and Pistol.]
DOLL. Jack, please, calm down. The scoundrel's gone. Ah, you brave little bastard of a villain, you!
HOSTESS. Aren't you hurt in the groin? I thought he made a nasty thrust at your belly.
[Enter Bardolph.]
FALSTAFF. Have you thrown him out of the door?
BARDOLPH. Yes, sir. The rascal's drunk. You've wounded him in the shoulder, sir.
FALSTAFF. The rascal, to defy me like that!

DOLL. Ah, you sweet little rogue, you! Oh, poor monkey, look how you sweat! Come, let me wipe your face. Come here, you bastard with the fat cheeks. Ah, rogue! Honestly, I love you. You're as brave as Hector of Troy, worth five Agamemnons, and ten times better than the Nine Worthies. Ah, villain!
FALSTAFF. The worthless slave! I'll toss the rogue in a blanket.
DOLL. Go on, if you dare, for your life. If you do, I'll toss you right back, between a pair of bed sheets.
[Enter Music.]
PAGE. The music has come, sir.
FALSTAFF. Let them play. Play, gentlemen. Sit on my knee, Doll. A bragging rascal of a slave! The rogue ran away from me like quicksilver.

DOLL. Yes, and you went after him like a church, big and slow. You bastard, you plump little Bartholomew Fair roast pig, when will you quit brawling by day and thrusting by night, and start patching up your old body for heaven?
[Enter, behind, Prince Henry and Poins, disguised as drawers.]
FALSTAFF. Hush, good Doll, don't talk like a death's-head. Don't tell me to remember my end.
DOLL. Tell me, what sort of man is the Prince?
FALSTAFF. A good, shallow young fellow. He'd have made a good pantler; he'd have chipped the crusts off the bread nicely.
DOLL. They say Poins has a good wit.
FALSTAFF. He, a good wit? Hang him, the baboon! His wit is as thick as Tewkesbury mustard. There's no more imagination in him than in a mallet.
DOLL. Why does the Prince love him so much, then?

FALSTAFF. Because their legs are the same size, and he plays quoits well, and eats conger eel and fennel, and drinks down candle-ends as flap-dragons, and rides the wild mare with the boys, and jumps over joint stools, and swears with a good grace, and wears his boots very smooth, like the sign of the Leg, and starts no quarrels by telling sensible stories. He has other playful skills like these, which show a weak mind and a strong body, and that's why the Prince admits him. The Prince himself is just the same. You couldn't get the weight of a hair between them on the scales.
PRINCE HENRY. Wouldn't this hub of a wheel, this knave, deserve to have his ears cut off?
POINS. Let's beat him in front of his whore.
PRINCE HENRY. Look at the withered old elder: his head is being scratched like a parrot's.
POINS. Isn't it strange that desire should outlive ability by so many years?
FALSTAFF. Kiss me, Doll.
PRINCE HENRY. Saturn and Venus in conjunction this year! What does the almanac say to that?
POINS. And see whether the fiery Trigon, his man, isn't lisping sweet talk to his master's old tablets, his notebook, his keeper of secrets.
FALSTAFF. You give me flattering kisses.
DOLL. On my word, I kiss you with a perfectly faithful heart.
FALSTAFF. I'm old, I'm old.
DOLL. I love you better than any one of those scurvy young boys.
FALSTAFF. What material do you want for a gown? I'll get money on Thursday; you'll have a cap tomorrow. A merry song! Come, it's getting late, we'll go to bed. You'll forget me when I'm gone.
DOLL. On my word, you'll set me crying if you say that. Just see if I ever dress up nicely until you come back. Well, wait and see how it ends.
FALSTAFF. Some sack, Francis.
PRINCE & POINS. Coming, coming, sir.
[Coming forward.]
FALSTAFF. Ha! A bastard son of the King's? And aren't you Poins's brother?
PRINCE HENRY. Why, you globe of sinful continents, what a life you lead!
FALSTAFF. A better one than yours. I'm a gentleman, you're a drawer.
PRINCE HENRY. Very true, sir, and I've come to draw you out by the ears.
HOSTESS. Oh, the Lord preserve your Grace! Truly, welcome to London. Now the Lord bless that sweet face of yours! Oh Jesus, have you come from Wales?
FALSTAFF. You bastard, you mad mixture of majesty, by this light, you flesh and corrupt blood, you're welcome.
DOLL. What? You fat fool, I scorn you.
POINS. My lord, he'll drive you out of your revenge and turn everything into a joke, if you don't strike while he's hot.
PRINCE HENRY. You bastard candle-mine, you mine of tallow, how vilely you spoke of me just now, in front of this honest, virtuous, decent gentlewoman!
HOSTESS. God bless your good heart! And so she is, on my word.
FALSTAFF. Did you hear me?
PRINCE HENRY. Yes, and you knew it, just as you did when you ran away at Gad's Hill. You knew I was right behind you, and you said it on purpose to test my patience.
FALSTAFF. No, no, no, not so. I didn't think you were within hearing.
PRINCE HENRY. Then I'll drive you to confess you insulted me on purpose, and then I'll know how to handle you.
FALSTAFF. No insult, Hal, on my honor, no insult.
PRINCE HENRY. Not to disparage me, and call me pantler and bread-chipper and I don't know what?
FALSTAFF. No insult, Hal.
POINS. No insult?

FALSTAFF. No insult, Ned, none in the world, honest Ned, none. I spoke ill of him in front of the wicked, so that the wicked wouldn't fall in love with you. In doing that, I played the part of a careful friend and a true subject, and your father should thank me for it. No insult, Hal; none, Ned; none, truly, boys, none.

PRINCE HENRY. See now whether pure fear and total cowardice don't make you wrong this virtuous gentlewoman just to make up with us. Is she among the wicked? Is your hostess here among the wicked? Or is your boy among the wicked? Or is honest Bardolph, whose zeal burns in his nose, among the wicked?
POINS. Answer, you dead elm, answer.

FALSTAFF. The devil has marked Bardolph down as lost beyond recovery, and his face is Lucifer's private kitchen, where he does nothing but roast malt-worms, meaning drunkards. As for the boy, there's a good angel about him, but the devil outbids him too.
PRINCE HENRY. And the women?
FALSTAFF. One of them is in hell already, and burns poor souls. The other one, I owe her money, and whether she's damned for that I don't know.
HOSTESS. No, I'm sure not.
FALSTAFF. No, I think you're not; I think you're cleared of that. But there's another charge against you, for letting meat be eaten in your house, against the law, and for that I think you'll howl.
HOSTESS. All tavern keepers do it. What's a joint of mutton or two in a whole Lent?
PRINCE HENRY. You, gentlewoman.
DOLL. What does your Grace say?
FALSTAFF. His grace says what his flesh rebels against.
[Peto knocks at door.]
HOSTESS. Who's knocking so loudly at the door? See to the door there, Francis.
[Enter Peto.]
PRINCE HENRY. Peto, what is it? What's the news?

PETO. The King your father is at Westminster, and twenty weak and exhausted messengers have come from the north. As I came along, I met and passed a dozen captains, bareheaded and sweating, knocking at the taverns and asking everyone for Sir John Falstaff.

PRINCE HENRY. By heaven, Poins, I feel very much to blame for wasting precious time so idly, when a storm of rebellion, like a south wind heavy with black vapor, is beginning to melt and drop on our bare, unprotected heads. Give me my sword and cloak. Falstaff, good night.
[Exeunt Prince Henry, Poins, Peto and Bardolph.]
FALSTAFF. Now comes the sweetest morsel of the night, and we have to leave and let it go unpicked.
[_Knocking within_.] Still more knocking at the door?
[Enter Bardolph.]
What is it now? What's the matter?
BARDOLPH. You have to go to court right away, sir. A dozen captains are waiting at the door for you.
FALSTAFF.
[_To the Page_.] Pay the musicians, boy. Farewell, hostess;

farewell, Doll. You see, my good girls, how men of merit are sought after. The man who deserves nothing can sleep while the man of action is called out. Farewell, good girls. If I'm not sent off in haste, I'll see you again before I go.
DOLL. I can't speak, I think my heart's about to burst. Well, sweet Jack, take care of yourself.
FALSTAFF. Farewell, farewell.
[Exeunt Falstaff and Bardolph.]
HOSTESS. Well, goodbye. I've known you these twenty-nine years, since pea-picking time. But a more honest and true-hearted man, well, goodbye.
BARDOLPH.
[Within.] Mistress Tearsheet!
HOSTESS. What's the matter?
BARDOLPH.
[_Within_.] Tell Mistress Tearsheet to come to my master.
HOSTESS. Oh, run, Doll, run; run, good Doll; come. She's coming, all blubbering. Yes, will you come, Doll?
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Westminster. The palace
paragraphs: [Enter the King in his nightgown, with a Page.]
HENRY IV. Go and call the Earls of Surrey and Warwick. But before they come, tell them to read over these letters and think them through carefully. Make haste.
[Exit Page.]

How many thousands of my poorest subjects are asleep at this very hour! Oh sleep, oh gentle sleep, nature's soft nurse, how have I scared you off? You no longer weigh my eyelids down or steep my senses in forgetfulness. Why do you lie in smoky huts instead, stretched out on rough straw beds and hushed to sleep by buzzing night-flies? Why not in the perfumed rooms of the great, under canopies of costly state, lulled by the sweetest music? Oh you dull god, why do you lie with the lowest in filthy beds, and leave the king's bed no better than a sentry box or a common alarm bell? Will you seal up the ship-boy's eyes high on the giddy mast, and rock his brain in the cradle of the rough, commanding surge, with the winds visiting him? Those winds seize the ruffian waves by their tops, curl their monstrous heads and hang them with deafening clamor in the slippery clouds, so that the uproar would wake death itself. Can you, partial sleep, give your rest to the wet sea-boy in an hour so wild, and then, in the calmest and stillest night, with every comfort and means besides, deny it to a king? Then lie down, you happy lowly! Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.
[Enter Warwick and Surrey.]
WARWICK. Many good mornings to your Majesty!
HENRY IV. Is it a good morning, lords?
WARWICK. It's one o'clock, and past.
HENRY IV. Why then, good morning to you all, my lords. Have you read the letters I sent you?
WARWICK. We have, my liege.
HENRY IV. Then you see how foul the body of our kingdom is, what rank diseases are growing in it, and how dangerously close to its heart.
WARWICK. It is only a body with a disorder so far. It can be restored to its former strength with good advice and a little medicine. My Lord Northumberland will soon be cooled.

HENRY IV. Oh God, if only one could read the book of fate and see the cycle of the ages! Mountains are made level, and the mainland, tired of solid firmness, melts itself into the sea. At other times the sandy girdle of the ocean is too wide for Neptune's hips. See how chance's mockeries and changes fill the cup of change with different liquors! Oh, if this were seen, the happiest young man, looking over his whole course, the perils he had passed and the troubles still to come, would shut the book, sit down and die. It's not ten years since Richard and Northumberland, great friends, feasted together, and two years after that they were at war. It is only eight years since this Percy was the man closest to my soul. He worked like a brother in my affairs and laid his love and his life under my foot. Yes, for my sake he even defied Richard to his face. But which of you was there —
[_To Warwick_.] You, cousin Nevil, if I remember rightly —

When Richard, his eyes brimful of tears, and rebuked and scolded by Northumberland, spoke these words, now proved a prophecy? "Northumberland, you ladder by which my cousin Bolingbroke climbs to my throne." Though then, God knows, I had no such intention, except that necessity had so bowed the state that greatness and I were forced to kiss. "The time will come," he went on, "the time will come when foul sin, gathering head, will break out in corruption." So he continued, foretelling the condition of these times and the division of our friendship.

WARWICK. There is a history in all men's lives that shows the nature of past times. If a man observes it, he can prophesy with near accuracy about the main course of things not yet born, which lie hidden in their seeds and weak beginnings. Such things are the hatching and brood of time. By this necessary pattern, King Richard could have made a perfect guess that great Northumberland, then false to him, would grow from that seed into a greater falseness, which would find no ground to take root in unless it were in you.
HENRY IV. Are these things necessities, then? Then let us meet them as necessities. And that very word cries out against us now. They say the bishop and Northumberland are fifty thousand strong.

WARWICK. It cannot be, my lord. Rumour doubles the numbers of what is feared, like a voice and its echo. Please, your Grace, go to bed. Upon my soul, my lord, the forces you have already sent out will bring in this prize very easily. To comfort you more, I have received sure word that Glendower is dead. Your Majesty has been ill for a fortnight, and these unseasonable hours must add to your sickness.
HENRY IV. I'll take your advice. And once these wars at home were settled, dear lords, we would go to the Holy Land.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Gloucestershire. Before Justice Shallow’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Shallow and Silence, meeting; Mouldy, Shadow, Wart, Feeble, Bullcalf, a Servant or two with them.]
SHALLOW. Come on, come on, come on. Give me your hand, sir, give me your hand. An early riser, by the cross! And how is my good cousin Silence?
SILENCE. Good morning, good cousin Shallow.
SHALLOW. And how is my cousin, your bedfellow? And your fairest daughter and mine, my goddaughter Ellen?
SILENCE. Alas, a black ousel, a dark blackbird, cousin Shallow!
SHALLOW. By yea and no, sir, I'll bet my cousin William has become a good scholar. He's still at Oxford, isn't he?
SILENCE. Indeed, sir, to my cost.
SHALLOW. Then he'll have to go to the Inns of Court soon. I was once at Clement's Inn, where I think they still talk about mad Shallow.
SILENCE. You were called "lusty Shallow" then, cousin.

SHALLOW. By the mass, I was called anything, and I would have done anything too, and thoroughly. There was me, and little John Doit of Staffordshire, and black George Barnes, and Francis Pickbone, and Will Squele, a Cotswold man. You wouldn't find four such swashbucklers again in all the Inns of Court. And I can tell you, we knew where the bona-robas were, the fine whores, and had the best of them all at our command. Jack Falstaff, now Sir John, was a boy then, page to Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk.
SILENCE. This Sir John, cousin, who's coming here soon about soldiers?

SHALLOW. The same Sir John, the very same. I saw him break Scoggin's head at the court gate, when he was a young scrap of a boy no taller than this. And the very same day I fought with one Sampson Stockfish, a fruiterer, behind Gray's Inn. Jesus, Jesus, the mad days I've spent! And to see how many of my old acquaintances are dead!
SILENCE. We shall all follow, cousin.
SHALLOW. Certain, it's certain, very sure, very sure. Death, as the Psalmist says, is certain for all; all shall die. What are good oxen going for at Stamford fair?
SILENCE. Truly, I wasn't there.
SHALLOW. Death is certain. Is old Double from your town still living?
SILENCE. Dead, sir.

SHALLOW. Jesus, Jesus, dead! He drew a good bow, and dead! He shot a fine shot. John of Gaunt loved him well, and bet a lot of money on him. Dead! He would have hit the bullseye at twelve score yards, and sent a forehand arrow fourteen or fourteen and a half score, so that it would have done a man's heart good to see. What are twenty ewes going for now?
SILENCE. It depends on what they are. Twenty good ewes may be worth ten pounds.
SHALLOW. And is old Double dead?
SILENCE. Here come two of Sir John Falstaff's men, I think.
[Enter Bardolph and one with him.]
SHALLOW. Good morning, honest gentlemen.
BARDOLPH. Please, which of you is Justice Shallow?
SHALLOW. I am Robert Shallow, sir, a poor squire of this county, and one of the King's justices of the peace. What can I do for you?
BARDOLPH. My captain, sir, sends you his regards. My captain, Sir John Falstaff, a brave gentleman, by heaven, and a most gallant leader.
SHALLOW. He greets me kindly, sir. I knew him as a good backsword man. How is the good knight? May I ask how my lady his wife is?
BARDOLPH. Sir, pardon me. A soldier is better accommodated than with a wife.

SHALLOW. That's well said, truly, sir, and well said indeed too. "Better accommodated!" It's good, yes indeed it is. Good phrases are surely, and always were, very commendable. "Accommodated." It comes from _accommodo_. Very good, a good phrase.

BARDOLPH. Pardon me, sir, I have heard the word. Phrase, do you call it? By this day, I don't know about "phrase," but I'll maintain with my sword that the word is a soldierly word, and a word of excellent command, by heaven. "Accommodated": that is when a man is, as they say, accommodated; or when a man is being, whereby he may be thought to be accommodated, which is an excellent thing.
SHALLOW. That's very right.
[Enter Falstaff.]
Look, here comes good Sir John. Give me your good hand, give me your worship's good hand. On my word, you look well and carry your years very well. Welcome, good Sir John.
FALSTAFF. I'm glad to see you well, good Master Robert Shallow. Master Surecard, I think?
SHALLOW. No, Sir John, it's my cousin Silence, who serves on the commission with me.
FALSTAFF. Good Master Silence, it suits you well to be a justice of the peace.
SILENCE. Your good worship is welcome.
FALSTAFF. Ugh, this is hot weather, gentlemen. Have you provided me with half a dozen fit men?
SHALLOW. Indeed we have, sir. Will you sit?
FALSTAFF. Let me see them, please.

SHALLOW. Where's the list? Where's the list? Where's the list? Let me see, let me see, let me see. So, so, so, so, so, so, so. Ah, there, sir: Ralph Mouldy! Let them step forward as I call them. Let them do so, let them do so. Let me see; where is Mouldy?
MOULDY. Here, if it please you.
SHALLOW. What do you think, Sir John? A well-built fellow, young, strong, and with good connections.
FALSTAFF. Is your name Mouldy?
MOULDY. Yes, if it please you.
FALSTAFF. All the more reason you were put to use.
SHALLOW. Ha, ha, ha! Most excellent, truly! Things that are mouldy lack use. Very rare and good, truly. Well said, Sir John, very well said.
FALSTAFF. Prick him, mark him down.

MOULDY. I was pricked well enough already, if you could have left me alone. My old wife will be ruined now, with nobody to do her farm work and her drudgery. You needn't have pricked me; there are other men fitter to go out than I am.
FALSTAFF. Come on. Quiet, Mouldy; you'll go. Mouldy, it's time you were used up.
MOULDY. Used up?
SHALLOW. Quiet, fellow, quiet. Stand aside. Do you know where you are? Now for the other, Sir John. Let me see: Simon Shadow!
FALSTAFF. Yes indeed, let me have him to sit under. He's likely to make a cold soldier.
SHALLOW. Where's Shadow?
SHADOW. Here, sir.
FALSTAFF. Shadow, whose son are you?
SHADOW. My mother's son, sir.
FALSTAFF. Your mother's son! Likely enough, and your father's shadow. So the son of the female is the shadow of the male. It's often so indeed, but with very little of the father's substance!
SHALLOW. Do you like him, Sir John?
FALSTAFF. Shadow will do for summer. Mark him down, for we need a number of shadows to fill up the muster-book.
SHALLOW. Thomas Wart!
FALSTAFF. Where is he?
WART. Here, sir.
FALSTAFF. Is your name Wart?
WART. Yes, sir.
FALSTAFF. You are a very ragged wart.
SHALLOW. Shall I mark him down, Sir John?
FALSTAFF. There's no need, for his clothes are built on his back, and the whole frame stands on pins. Don't prick him any more.
SHALLOW. Ha, ha, ha! You can do it, sir, you can do it. I commend you. Francis Feeble!
FEEBLE. Here, sir.
FALSTAFF. What's your trade, Feeble?
FEEBLE. A woman's tailor, sir.
SHALLOW. Shall I mark him down, sir?
FALSTAFF. You may. But if he had been a man's tailor, he'd have pricked you. Will you make as many holes in an enemy's battle line as you've made in a woman's petticoat?
FEEBLE. I'll do my best, sir; you can ask no more.

FALSTAFF. Well said, good woman's tailor! Well said, courageous Feeble! You'll be as valiant as the wrathful dove or the most magnanimous mouse. Mark down the woman's tailor. Well, Master Shallow, deep, Master Shallow.
FEEBLE. I wish Wart could have gone, sir.

FALSTAFF. I wish you were a man's tailor, so that you could mend him and make him fit to go. I can't put him in as a private soldier, when I'm the leader of so many thousands. Let that be enough, most forcible Feeble.
FEEBLE. It shall be enough, sir.
FALSTAFF. I'm obliged to you, reverend Feeble. Who's next?
SHALLOW. Peter Bullcalf of the green!
FALSTAFF. Yes indeed, let's see Bullcalf.
BULLCALF. Here, sir.
FALSTAFF. By God, a likely fellow! Come, prick Bullcalf for me, mark him down, until he roars again.
BULLCALF. Oh Lord! My good lord captain —
FALSTAFF. What, do you roar before you're pricked?
BULLCALF. Oh Lord, sir, I'm a sick man.
FALSTAFF. What disease have you?
BULLCALF. A damned cold, sir, a cough, sir, that I caught ringing the bells for the King's business on his coronation day, sir.
FALSTAFF. Come, you'll go to the wars in a gown. We'll get rid of your cold, and I'll make sure your friends ring the bells for you. Is that everyone?
SHALLOW. Two more have been called than your number. You may have only four here, sir; and so, please, come in with me to dinner.
FALSTAFF. Come, I'll go and drink with you, but I can't stay for dinner. I'm glad to see you, on my word, Master Shallow.
SHALLOW. Oh, Sir John, do you remember when we lay all night in the windmill in Saint George's Field?
FALSTAFF. No more of that, good Master Shallow, no more of that.
SHALLOW. Ha, it was a merry night. And is Jane Nightwork alive?
FALSTAFF. She lives, Master Shallow.
SHALLOW. She never could stand me.
FALSTAFF. Never, never; she always said she couldn't bear Master Shallow.
SHALLOW. By the mass, I could anger her to the heart. She was a bona-roba then. Does she hold her own well?
FALSTAFF. Old, old, Master Shallow.
