SHALLOW. No, she must be old; she can't help being old. Certainly she's old, and she had Robin Nightwork by old Nightwork before I came to Clement's Inn.
SILENCE. That's fifty-five years ago.
SHALLOW. Ha, cousin Silence, if only you had seen what this knight and I have seen! Ha, Sir John, did I say well?
FALSTAFF. We have heard the chimes at midnight, Master Shallow.

SHALLOW. That we have, that we have, that we have; truly, Sir John, we have. Our watchword was "Hem, boys!" Come, let's go to dinner; come, let's go to dinner. Jesus, the days we have seen! Come, come.
[Exeunt Falstaff, Shallow and Silence.]

BULLCALF. Good Master Corporate Bardolph, be my friend. And here are four Harry ten-shilling pieces in French crowns for you. In very truth, sir, I'd as soon be hanged as go. And yet, for my own part, sir, I don't care. It's only that I'm unwilling, and for my own part I want to stay with my friends; otherwise, sir, I wouldn't care, for my own part, so much.
BARDOLPH. Go on, stand aside.
MOULDY. And, good Master Corporal Captain, for my old wife's sake, be my friend. She has nobody to do anything for her when I'm gone, and she is old and can't help herself. You shall have forty, sir.
BARDOLPH. Go on, stand aside.

FEEBLE. On my word, I don't care. A man can only die once. We owe God a death. I'll never have a base mind. If it's my destiny, so be it; if not, so be it. No man is too good to serve his prince, and let it go which way it will, the man who dies this year is excused from the next.
BARDOLPH. Well said, you're a good fellow.
FEEBLE. Truly, I'll have no base mind.
[Enter Falstaff and the Justices.]
FALSTAFF. Come, sir, which men shall I have?
SHALLOW. Four, whichever you please.
BARDOLPH. Sir, a word with you. I have three pounds to free Mouldy and Bullcalf.
FALSTAFF. All right, good.
SHALLOW. Come, Sir John, which four will you have?
FALSTAFF. You choose for me.
SHALLOW. Why, then: Mouldy, Bullcalf, Feeble and Shadow.
FALSTAFF. Mouldy and Bullcalf: you, Mouldy, stay at home until you're past service; and you, Bullcalf, grow until you're ready for it. I'll have none of you.
SHALLOW. Sir John, Sir John, don't wrong yourself. They're your likeliest men, and I want you served with the best.

FALSTAFF. Will you tell me, Master Shallow, how to choose a man? Do I care about the limb, the sinews, the stature, the bulk and big appearance of a man? Give me the spirit, Master Shallow. Here's Wart. You see what a ragged appearance he has. He'll load and fire for you with the motion of a pewterer's hammer, and come off and on guard faster than the man who hauls the brewer's bucket up on its beam. And this half-faced fellow Shadow: give me this man. He presents no target to the enemy; the foe might as well aim at the edge of a penknife. And for a retreat, how swiftly this Feeble, the woman's tailor, will run off! Oh, give me the spare men, and spare me the big ones. Put a caliver in Wart's hand, Bardolph.
BARDOLPH. Hold it, Wart. Traverse. Thas, thas, thas.

FALSTAFF. Come, handle your caliver for me. So, very well, go on, very good, exceedingly good. Oh, give me always a little, lean, old, chapped, bald shot. Well said, truly, Wart. You're a good scab. Here, there's a sixpence for you.

SHALLOW. He's not master of his craft; he doesn't do it right. I remember at Mile-End Green, when I lay at Clement's Inn (I was Sir Dagonet in Arthur's show then), there was a little nimble fellow who would handle his piece like this. He'd go about and about, and come in and come in. "Rah, tah, tah," he'd say. "Bounce," he'd say; and away he'd go again, and again he'd come. I'll never see such a fellow.

FALSTAFF. These fellows will do well. Master Shallow, God keep you. Master Silence, I won't use many words with you. Farewell, gentlemen both. I thank you. I have to go a dozen miles tonight. Bardolph, give the soldiers coats.
SHALLOW. Sir John, the Lord bless you! God prosper your affairs! God send us peace! When you return, visit our house, and let our old acquaintance be renewed. Perhaps I'll go with you to court.
FALSTAFF. By God, I wish you would, Master Shallow.
SHALLOW. Well, I've given you my word. God keep you.

FALSTAFF. Farewell, gentle gentlemen. [_Exeunt Justices_.] On, Bardolph, lead the men away. [_Exeunt Bardolph, recruits, &c._] When I come back, I'll skim these justices. I can see the bottom of Justice Shallow. Lord, Lord, how prone we old men are to the vice of lying! This starved justice has done nothing but prattle to me about the wildness of his youth and the feats he did around Turnbull Street, and every third word is a lie, more reliably paid to the listener than the Turk's tribute. I remember him at Clement's Inn, like a man made after supper out of a cheese-paring. Naked, he was just like a forked radish with a head fancifully carved on it with a knife. He was so wretched that to any dull eye his shape was invisible. He was the very spirit of famine, yet lecherous as a monkey, and the whores called him mandrake. He always came at the rear of the fashion, and he sang to the over-used housewives the tunes he'd heard the carters whistle, and swore they were his own fancies or his good-nights. And now this Vice's dagger has become a squire, and talks as familiarly of John of Gaunt as if he'd been his sworn brother. I'll swear he never saw Gaunt but once, in the tilt-yard, and then he got his head broken for crowding among the marshal's men. I saw it, and told John of Gaunt he had beaten his own name, for you could have thrust him and all his clothes into an eel-skin. The case of a treble oboe was a mansion for him, a court. And now he has land and cattle. Well, I'll get acquainted with him if I return, and it will go hard but I'll make him a philosopher's two stones for me. If the young dace is bait for the old pike, I see no reason in the law of nature why I shouldn't snap at him. Let time shape things, and that's the end.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — Yorkshire. Gaultree Forest
paragraphs: [Enter the Archbishop of York, Mowbray, Hastings and others.]
ARCHBISHOP. What's this forest called?
HASTINGS. It's Gaultree Forest, if it please your Grace.
ARCHBISHOP. Stop here, my lords, and send scouts out to find how many enemies we face.
HASTINGS. We've already sent them.

ARCHBISHOP. Good. My friends and brothers in this great business, I have to tell you that I've just received a recent letter from Northumberland. Its message, in cold substance, is this. He wishes he could have brought an army worthy of his rank, but he couldn't raise one. So he has withdrawn to Scotland to let his growing fortunes ripen. He ends with heartfelt prayers that our attempt will survive the danger and the fearful meeting with our opponents.
MOWBRAY. So the hopes we had in him hit bottom and smash to pieces.
[Enter a Messenger.]
HASTINGS. Now, what news?
MESSENGER. West of this forest, barely a mile away, the enemy is advancing in fine order. Judging by the ground they cover, I'd say their number is at or near thirty thousand.
MOWBRAY. Exactly the size we reckoned they'd be. Let's march on and face them in the field.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
ARCHBISHOP. What well-equipped commander is this, coming at us?
MOWBRAY. I think it's my Lord of Westmoreland.
WESTMORELAND. Greetings and good health from our general, the prince, Lord John, Duke of Lancaster.
ARCHBISHOP. Speak, my Lord of Westmoreland, and speak in peace. What brings you here?

WESTMORELAND. Then, my lord, I address the main part of my speech to your Grace. Suppose rebellion came as itself, in base and wretched mobs, led by bloodthirsty youths, guarded by rags, and backed by boys and beggary. Suppose, I say, that this damned uprising showed itself in its own true, natural and proper shape. Then you, reverend father, and these noble lords would not be here to dress up the ugly form of base and bloody insurrection with your fine honors. But you, Lord Archbishop, have a see kept up by civil peace. Peace's silver hand has touched your beard, and peace has taught you your learning and your letters. Your white robes stand for innocence. You are the dove, the very blessed spirit of peace. So why do you so badly translate yourself out of the gracious language of peace into the harsh and rowdy tongue of war? You turn your books into graves, your ink into blood, your pens into lances, and your holy tongue into a loud trumpet and a call to arms!

ARCHBISHOP. Why do I do this? That's the question. Briefly, here's why. We are all sick. Through our overindulgence and idle hours we have brought ourselves into a burning fever, and we must be bled for it. Our late King Richard caught this same disease and died of it. But, my most noble Lord of Westmoreland, I don't set myself up here as a doctor. Nor do I march in among crowds of soldiers as an enemy of peace. I only play at fearsome war for a while, to put on a diet minds made sick by too much happiness, and to purge the blockages that are starting to clog our very veins of life. Let me say it more plainly. I have weighed fairly, in an even balance, what wrongs our arms may do and what wrongs we suffer, and I find our grievances heavier than our offences. We see which way the stream of time is running. We are driven out of our quiet place there by the rough torrent of events. We have a summary of all our grievances, to show in written articles when the time is right. We offered it to the King long before this, and no petition could win us a hearing. When we are wronged and want to lay out our grievances, we are denied access to his person, and denied by the very men who have wronged us most. The dangers of recent days, whose memory is still written on the earth in blood you can still see, and the examples of every passing minute that confront us now, have driven us into these unbecoming arms. We aren't here to break the peace or any branch of it. We are here to establish a peace that is a peace indeed, in name and in nature.

WESTMORELAND. When was your appeal ever refused? How has the King ever injured you? Which peer has been bribed to grate on you, so that you should put a holy seal on this lawless, bloody book of forged rebellion, and bless the bitter edge of an uprising?
ARCHBISHOP. My brother general, I make my particular quarrel the commonwealth, and the cruelty done within my own household to a brother born.
WESTMORELAND. There's no need for any such remedy. Or if there were, it wouldn't be your business.
MOWBRAY. Why isn't it his business in part, and ours as well, who feel the bruises of the past days and suffer the conditions of these times, which lay a heavy and unequal hand on our honors?

WESTMORELAND. Oh, my good Lord Mowbray, read the times according to their necessities and you'll say yourself that it is the times, and not the King, that do you injury. And as for you, it doesn't appear to me, from the King or from the present time, that you have an inch of ground to build a grievance on. Weren't you restored to all the estates of the Duke of Norfolk, your noble and well-remembered father?

MOWBRAY. What did my father lose, in honor, that has to be revived and breathed into me? King Richard loved him. But as matters stood then, he was forced, whether he liked it or not, to banish him. Think of that day, when Henry Bolingbroke and my father sat mounted and fired up in their saddles, their neighing horses daring the spur, their lances at the ready, their visors down, their fiery eyes sparkling through the sights of steel, and the loud trumpet blowing them together. Then, when nothing could have held my father back from Bolingbroke's chest, oh, then the King threw down his baton, and his own life hung on the staff he threw. In throwing it down he threw away himself, and the lives of all those who, by indictment and by the sword, have since come to grief under Bolingbroke.

WESTMORELAND. You speak, Lord Mowbray, without knowing what you say. The Earl of Hereford was then reputed the most valiant gentleman in England. Who knows on whom fortune would have smiled? But if your father had been the victor there, he'd never have carried it out of Coventry. The whole country cried out in one voice against him. All their prayers and their love were set on Hereford, whom they doted on and blessed and favored, in truth more than they did the King. But this is a mere digression from my purpose. I come here from our princely general to learn your grievances, and to tell you from his Grace that he will give you a hearing. And wherever it shows that your demands are just, you shall have them, with everything set aside that might so much as make anyone think of you as enemies.
MOWBRAY. But he has forced us to make this offer necessary, and it comes from policy, not love.

WESTMORELAND. Mowbray, you are too presumptuous to take it that way. This offer comes from mercy, not from fear. Look, our army lies within sight, on my honor, far too confident to let in any thought of fear. Our force has more men of name than yours, our men are more skilled in arms, our armor is just as strong, and our cause is the best. So it's reasonable that our hearts should be as good. Don't say, then, that our offer is forced.
MOWBRAY. Well, as far as I'm concerned we'll allow no parley.
WESTMORELAND. That only shows the shame of your offence. A rotten case can't stand being handled.
HASTINGS. Does Prince John have a full commission, with ample authority from his father, to hear what terms we insist on and to decide on them absolutely?
WESTMORELAND. That is understood, in the general's name. I wonder you ask so slight a question.

ARCHBISHOP. Then take this paper, my Lord of Westmoreland, for it contains our general grievances. Let each separate article in it be put right. Then everyone who belongs to our cause, here and elsewhere, and who is bound to this action, will be acquitted in true and substantial form. Our wishes will be carried out at once for us and for our purposes, which are limited to this. Then we will come back within our proper bounds, in fear of the law, and join our forces to the arm of peace.

WESTMORELAND. I'll show this to the general. Please, lords, let us meet in sight of both our armies. Either we'll end in peace, which God grant! Or we'll call the swords to the place of the dispute, to decide it.
ARCHBISHOP. My lord, we will do so.
[Exit Westmoreland.]
MOWBRAY. Something in my heart tells me that no terms of our peace can last.
HASTINGS. Don't fear that. If we can make our peace on terms as broad and absolute as our conditions will insist on, our peace will stand as firm as rocky mountains.

MOWBRAY. Yes, but they'll value our case this way. Every slight and falsely derived cause, every idle, petty and frivolous reason, will be made by the King to taste of this action. So even if our royal loyalties were martyrs of love, we would be winnowed by so rough a wind that even our good grain would seem as light as chaff, and good and bad could not be told apart.

ARCHBISHOP. No, no, my lord. Note this: the King is tired of dainty, nitpicking grievances. He has found that ending one doubt by death revives two greater ones in the heirs of the living. So he will wipe his tablet clean and keep no tell-tale to his memory that could repeat and record his loss and bring it to new remembrance. He knows very well that he cannot weed this land as precisely as his suspicions demand. His foes are so rooted in among his friends that when he pulls to uproot an enemy, he loosens and shakes a friend as well. So this land is like an offensive wife who has enraged her husband into raising his hand to strike. As he is striking, she holds up their infant, and he hangs his resolved punishment in the very arm that was raised to carry it out.
HASTINGS. Besides, the King has worn out all his rods on recent offenders, so that he now lacks the very instruments of punishment. His power, like a lion without fangs, may threaten but cannot hold.

ARCHBISHOP. That's very true. And so, my good Lord Marshal, be assured that if we make our reconciliation well now, our peace will be like a broken limb that has knit together: it will grow stronger for the breaking.
MOWBRAY. So be it. Here my Lord of Westmoreland has come back.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
WESTMORELAND. The prince is close at hand. Will your lordship please to meet his Grace at the midpoint between our armies?
MOWBRAY. Your Grace of York, in God's name, then set forward.
ARCHBISHOP. Go ahead and greet his Grace. My lord, we're coming.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Another part of the forest
paragraphs: [Enter, from one side, Mowbray, attended; afterwards, the Archbishop, Hastings, and others; from the other side, Prince John of Lancaster, and Westmoreland; Officers, and others with them.]

LANCASTER. Well met here, my cousin Mowbray. Good day to you, gentle Lord Archbishop, and to you, Lord Hastings, and to all. My Lord of York, you looked better when your flock, gathered by the church bell, sat around you to hear you explain the holy text with reverence. It's worse to see you now as an iron man, cheering a mob of rebels with your drum, turning the Word into a sword and life into death. A man who sits close to a monarch's heart and ripens in the sunshine of his favor might abuse the king's trust. Alas, what mischief he could start in the shadow of such greatness! With you, Lord Bishop, it is just so. Who hasn't heard how deep you were in the books of God? You were the speaker for God in our parliament, the imagined voice of God himself, the very go-between linking the grace and holiness of heaven with our dull workings. Oh, who will believe that you aren't misusing the reverence of your office? You use the favor and grace of heaven for dishonorable deeds, the way a false favorite uses his prince's name. Under a counterfeit zeal for God, you have raised the subjects of God's substitute, my father, and swarmed them up here, against the peace of heaven and against him.

ARCHBISHOP. Good my Lord of Lancaster, I'm not here against your father's peace. But as I told my Lord of Westmoreland, these disordered times, as plain sense shows, crowd and crush us into this monstrous shape to keep our safety up. I sent your Grace the details and particulars of our grievance. It was shoved aside from the court with scorn, and that is how this Hydra, this child of war, was born. Its dangerous eyes may well be charmed asleep by granting our most just and rightful desires. Then, cured of this madness, it will stoop tamely to the foot of majesty in true obedience.
MOWBRAY. If not, we're ready to try our fortunes to the last man.

HASTINGS. And even if we fall here, we have reinforcements to back our attempt. If they fail, others will back them. So success in this mischief will be born anew, and heir after heir will hold up this quarrel as long as England has children.
LANCASTER. You are too shallow, Hastings, much too shallow, to sound the depths of the times to come.
WESTMORELAND. Will it please your Grace to answer them directly, and say how far you approve their articles?

LANCASTER. I approve them all and fully allow them. And I swear here, by the honor of my blood, that my father's purposes have been misunderstood, and that some around him have stretched his meaning and authority too freely. My lord, these grievances will be quickly set right. Upon my soul, they will. If this pleases you, send your forces back to their home counties, as we will ours. And here, between the armies, let's drink together as friends and embrace, so that all their eyes can carry home those tokens of our restored love and friendship.
ARCHBISHOP. I take your princely word for these remedies.
LANCASTER. I give it to you, and will keep my word. And on that, I drink to your Grace.
HASTINGS. Go, captain, and give the army this news of peace. Let them have their pay, and part. I know it will please them. Hurry, captain.
[Exit Officer.]
ARCHBISHOP. To you, my noble Lord of Westmoreland.
WESTMORELAND. I pledge your Grace. And if you knew what pains I took to bring about this present peace, you would drink freely. But my love for you will show itself more openly later.
ARCHBISHOP. I don't doubt you.
WESTMORELAND. I'm glad of it. Health to my lord and gentle cousin Mowbray.
MOWBRAY. You wish me health at a very good time, for I've suddenly become somewhat ill.
ARCHBISHOP. Against bad luck men are always merry, but heaviness comes before good outcomes.
WESTMORELAND. Then be merry, cousin, since sudden sorrow serves to say this: "Some good thing comes tomorrow."
ARCHBISHOP. Believe me, I'm exceedingly light in spirit.
MOWBRAY. So much the worse, if your own rule is true.
[Shouts within.]
LANCASTER. The word of peace has been delivered. Listen how they shout!
MOWBRAY. This would have been cheering after a victory.
ARCHBISHOP. A peace is like a conquest in nature, for then both sides are nobly beaten and neither side loses.
LANCASTER. Go, my lord. And let our army be dismissed too.
[Exit Westmoreland.]
And, my good lord, if you please, let our troops march past us, so we can look over the men we would have fought.
ARCHBISHOP. Go, good Lord Hastings, and before they're dismissed, have them march by.
[Exit Hastings.]
LANCASTER. I trust, lords, we'll sleep together tonight.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
Now, cousin, why is our army standing still?
WESTMORELAND. The leaders, having orders from you to stand, won't leave until they hear you speak.
LANCASTER. They know their duties.
[Enter Hastings.]

HASTINGS. My lord, our army is already dispersed. Like young bullocks let out of the yoke, they've gone off in every direction, east, west, north and south. Or like a school let out, each one hurries toward his home and playground.
WESTMORELAND. Good news, my Lord Hastings. For that I arrest you, traitor, for high treason. And you, Lord Archbishop, and you, Lord Mowbray, I arrest both of you for capital treason.
MOWBRAY. Is this proceeding just and honorable?
WESTMORELAND. Is your assembly just and honorable?
ARCHBISHOP. Will you break your faith like this?

LANCASTER. I pledged you none. I promised you a remedy for those same grievances you complained of, and by my honor I will carry it out with most Christian care. But as for you, rebels, expect to taste the punishment due for rebellion and acts like yours. You started these arms very foolishly: you were brought here by folly and foolishly sent home. Strike up our drums, chase the scattered stragglers. God, and not we, has fought safely today. Some of you, guard these traitors to the block of death, treason's true bed and the place where it gives up breath.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — Another part of the forest
paragraphs: [Alarum. Excursions. Enter Falstaff and Colevile, meeting.]
FALSTAFF. What's your name, sir? What's your rank, and where are you from, please?
COLEVILE. I'm a knight, sir, and my name is Colevile of the Dale.

FALSTAFF. Well then, Colevile is your name, knight is your rank, and the Dale is your place. From now on Colevile will still be your name, but traitor will be your rank and the dungeon your place, and that's a place deep enough. So you'll still be Colevile of the Dale.
COLEVILE. Aren't you Sir John Falstaff?

FALSTAFF. As good a man as he, sir, whoever I am. Do you yield, sir, or do I have to sweat for you? If I do sweat, the drops will be your friends' tears, and they'll be weeping for your death. So work up some fear and trembling, and show respect to my mercy.
COLEVILE. I think you are Sir John Falstaff, and on that thought I yield to you.

FALSTAFF. I have a whole school of tongues in this belly of mine, and not one of them says any word but my name. If I only had a belly of any reasonable size, I'd simply be the most active fellow in Europe. My womb, my womb, my womb is my undoing. Here comes our general.
[Enter Prince John of Lancaster, Westmoreland, Blunt, and others.]
LANCASTER. The heat is over. Don't pursue any further. Call in the troops, good cousin Westmoreland.
[Exit Westmoreland.]
Now, Falstaff, where have you been all this time? You show up when everything is over. On my life, these late tricks of yours will break some gallows' back one of these days.

FALSTAFF. I'd be sorry, my lord, if it were any other way. I've never known anything but rebuke and reproach as the reward of courage. Do you take me for a swallow, an arrow, or a bullet? In my poor old frame, do I have the speed of thought? I've hurried here to the very last inch of what's possible. I've worn out a hundred and eighty-odd post horses. And here, travel-stained as I am, with my pure and spotless valor I've captured Sir John Colevile of the Dale, a most furious knight and brave enemy. But what of that? He saw me, and he yielded. So I can fairly say, like that hook-nosed fellow of Rome, "I came, I saw, I conquered."
LANCASTER. That was more his courtesy than your deserving.

FALSTAFF. I don't know. Here he is, and here I hand him over. And I beg your Grace, let it be entered in the record with the rest of today's deeds. If not, by the Lord, I'll have it in a ballad of its own, with my own picture at the top of it and Colevile kissing my foot. And if I'm forced to that course, then unless you all look like gilded twopenny coins next to me, and I outshine you in the clear sky of fame as much as the full moon outshines the cinders of the heavens, which look like pinheads beside her, don't believe the word of a nobleman. So give me my due, and let merit rise.
LANCASTER. Yours is too heavy to rise.
FALSTAFF. Then let it shine.
LANCASTER. Yours is too thick to shine.
FALSTAFF. Let it do something, my good lord, that will do me some good, and call it what you like.
LANCASTER. Is your name Colevile?
COLEVILE. It is, my lord.
LANCASTER. You're a famous rebel, Colevile.
FALSTAFF. And a famous true subject took him.
COLEVILE. I am a rebel, my lord, only as my betters are, who led me here. If they had listened to me, you would have won them at a higher price than you have.
FALSTAFF. I don't know how they sold themselves, but you, like a kind fellow, gave yourself away for nothing, and I thank you for you.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
LANCASTER. Now, have you called off the pursuit?
WESTMORELAND. The retreat has been sounded and the killing halted.
LANCASTER. Send Colevile and his accomplices to York, for immediate execution. Blunt, take him away, and make sure you guard him well.
[Exeunt Blunt and others with Colevile.]

And now let's head for the court, my lords. I hear the King my father is very sick. Our news will go ahead of us to his Majesty, and you, cousin, will carry it to comfort him. We'll follow you with steady speed.
FALSTAFF. My lord, I beg you to give me leave to go through Gloucestershire, and when you come to court, please stand my good lord and speak well of me.
LANCASTER. Farewell, Falstaff. In my position I'll speak better of you than you deserve.
[Exeunt all but Falstaff.]

FALSTAFF. I wish you had a little wit. It would be better than your dukedom. Honestly, this sober-blooded young boy doesn't like me, and a man can't make him laugh. But that's no wonder: he drinks no wine. None of these demure boys ever amounts to anything. Thin drink cools their blood too much, and they eat so many fish meals that they fall into a kind of male green-sickness. Then, when they marry, they father girls. They're generally fools and cowards, which some of us would be too, if not for the heat. A good sherry-sack does two things. First, it rises up into my brain and dries up all the foolish, dull and curdled vapors that surround it. It makes the brain sharp, quick, inventive, and full of nimble, fiery, delightful shapes. Handed over to the voice, the tongue, which is its birth, those shapes turn into excellent wit. The second property of excellent sherry is that it warms the blood. Before, the blood was cold and settled, and it left the liver white and pale, which is the badge of weakness and cowardice. But sherry warms it and makes it run from the inner parts to the extremities. It lights up the face, which, like a beacon, warns all the rest of this little kingdom, man, to arm. Then the vital commoners and the lesser inland spirits all muster to their captain, the heart. Swollen and proud with this retinue, the heart does any deed of courage, and this valor comes of sherry. So skill with a weapon is nothing without sack, because sack sets it to work. And learning is merely a hoard of gold guarded by a devil, until sack puts it to use and into action. That's why Prince Harry is valiant. The cold blood he naturally inherited from his father, he has treated like lean, barren, bare land. He has fertilized, farmed and tilled it with the excellent effort of drinking good sherry, and plenty of it, until he's become very hot and valiant. If I had a thousand sons, the first human principle I would teach them would be to swear off thin drinks and give themselves to sack.
[Enter Bardolph.]
How now, Bardolph?
BARDOLPH. The army is all discharged and gone.

FALSTAFF. Let them go. I'll go through Gloucestershire, and there I'll visit Master Robert Shallow, Esquire. I already have him softening like wax between my finger and thumb, and soon I'll seal a deal with him. Come along.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — Westminster. The Jerusalem Chamber
paragraphs: [Enter the King, Warwick, Thomas Duke of Clarence and Humphrey Duke of Gloucester and others.]

HENRY IV. Now, lords, if God gives a successful end to this conflict that bleeds at our doors, we will lead our youth on to higher fields and draw no swords except sanctified ones. Our navy is ready, our army gathered, our deputies well installed for our absence, and everything lies level with our wish. We only lack a little personal strength. So let us wait until these rebels now in the field come under the yoke of government.
WARWICK. We don't doubt that your Majesty will soon have both.
HENRY IV. Humphrey, my son of Gloucester, where is the Prince your brother?
GLOUCESTER. I think he's gone hunting at Windsor, my lord.
HENRY IV. And who is with him?
GLOUCESTER. I don't know, my lord.
HENRY IV. Isn't his brother Thomas of Clarence with him?
GLOUCESTER. No, my good lord, he's here in your presence.
CLARENCE. What does my lord and father want?

HENRY IV. Nothing but good for you, Thomas of Clarence. How is it that you aren't with the Prince your brother? He loves you, and you neglect him, Thomas. You have a better place in his affection than all your brothers. Cherish it, my boy. After I am dead, you may do noble service by mediating between his greatness and your other brothers. So don't leave him out, don't dull his love, and don't lose the advantage of his favor by seeming cold or careless of his wishes. He is gracious if he is treated carefully. He has a tear for pity and a hand open as the day for melting charity. Yet when he's angered, he's flint, as moody as winter and as sudden as the gusts that freeze in the first part of a spring day. So his temper must be carefully watched. Scold him for his faults, and do it respectfully, when you see his blood inclined to mirth. But when he's moody, give him time and room, until his passions, like a whale stranded on the shore, wear themselves out with their thrashing. Learn this, Thomas, and you'll prove a shelter to your friends, a golden hoop to bind your brothers together. Then the united vessel of their blood, mixed with the poison of whispered suggestions, as the age will inevitably pour in, will never leak, even though it ferments as strongly as aconite or hasty gunpowder.
CLARENCE. I'll watch him with all care and love.
HENRY IV. Why aren't you at Windsor with him, Thomas?
CLARENCE. He's not there today. He's dining in London.
HENRY IV. And who is with him? Can you tell me that?
CLARENCE. Poins, and others of his constant followers.

HENRY IV. The richest soil is the most prone to weeds. And he, the noble image of my youth, is overgrown with them. So my grief reaches beyond the hour of death. The blood weeps from my heart when I picture in my mind the unguided days and rotten times that you will see when I am sleeping with my ancestors. For when his headstrong riot has no curb, when rage and hot blood are his counselors, when means and lavish manners meet together, oh, with what wings will his desires fly toward facing danger and toward decay!

WARWICK. My gracious lord, you look far beyond him. The prince is only studying his companions, like a foreign language. To gain the language, it's necessary to look at and learn even the most immodest word. Once learned, as your Highness knows, it has no further use except to be known and hated. In the same way, like crude words, the Prince will, when the time is ripe, cast off his followers. Their memory will live on as a pattern or measure by which his Grace will judge the lives of others, turning past evils into advantages.
HENRY IV. It's seldom that the bee leaves her honeycomb in the dead carcass.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
Who's here? Westmoreland?

WESTMORELAND. Health to my sovereign, and new happiness added to what I'm here to deliver! Prince John your son kisses your Grace's hand. Mowbray, Bishop Scroop, Hastings and all of them are brought to the correction of your law. There's not a rebel's sword unsheathed now, and Peace puts forth her olive branch everywhere. Your Highness can read at more leisure how this action was carried out, with every step in detail.
HENRY IV. Oh Westmoreland, you are a summer bird, which always sings, even late in winter, of the day coming up.
[Enter Harcourt.]
Look, here's more news.

HARCOURT. May heaven keep your Majesty from enemies, and when they stand against you, may they fall like those I've come to tell you about! The Earl of Northumberland and Lord Bardolph, with a great force of English and Scots, have been overthrown by the sheriff of Yorkshire. The manner and true order of the fight is set out in full in this packet, if it please you.

HENRY IV. And why should this good news make me sick? Will Fortune never come with both hands full, but always write her fair words in the foulest letters? She either gives an appetite and no food, which is what the poor are like when they're healthy, or else a feast and takes away the appetite, which is what the rich are like, who have plenty and don't enjoy it. I should rejoice now at this happy news, and now my sight fails and my brain is giddy. Oh me! Come near me, now I'm very ill.
GLOUCESTER. Take comfort, your Majesty!
CLARENCE. Oh my royal father!
WESTMORELAND. My sovereign lord, cheer up, look up.
WARWICK. Be patient, princes. You know these fits are very ordinary with his Highness. Stand back from him, give him air, and he'll soon be well.

CLARENCE. No, no, he can't hold out against these pangs for long. The constant care and labor of his mind has worn the wall that should hold it in so thin that life looks through it and will break out.

GLOUCESTER. The people frighten me, for they've noticed fatherless heirs and loathsome births of nature. The seasons change their ways, as if the year had found some months asleep and leaped over them.
CLARENCE. The river has flowed three times with no ebb between. And the old folk, time's doting chroniclers, say it did the same a little before our great-grandfather Edward fell sick and died.
WARWICK. Speak lower, princes, for the King is recovering.
GLOUCESTER. This apoplexy will certainly be his end.
HENRY IV. I beg you, lift me up and carry me from here into some other chamber. Gently, please.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — Another chamber
paragraphs: [The King lying on a bed. Clarence, Gloucester, Warwick and others in attendance.]
HENRY IV. Let there be no noise, my kind friends, unless some soft, gentle hand will play quiet music to soothe my weary spirit.
WARWICK. Call for the music in the other room.
HENRY IV. Put the crown here on my pillow, beside me.
CLARENCE. His eyes are hollow, and he is changing fast.
WARWICK. Quiet, quiet!
[Enter Prince Henry.]
PRINCE HENRY. Who has seen the Duke of Clarence?
CLARENCE. I'm here, brother, and heavy-hearted.
PRINCE HENRY. What, rain indoors and none outside? How is the King?
GLOUCESTER. Very ill.
PRINCE HENRY. Has he heard the good news yet? Tell him.
GLOUCESTER. He was much changed when he heard it.
PRINCE HENRY. If joy has made him sick, he'll get well without any medicine.
WARWICK. Not so loud, my lords. Gentle prince, speak softly. The King your father wants to sleep.
CLARENCE. Let's go into the other room.
WARWICK. Will your Grace come with us?
PRINCE HENRY. No, I'll stay and keep watch by the King.
[Exeunt all but the Prince.]

Why does the crown lie there on his pillow, when it makes such an uncomfortable bedfellow? Oh, polished torment! Golden worry! You keep the gates of sleep wide open through so many nights of watching. Sleep beside it now, but not as soundly or as sweetly as the man with a plain nightcap tied around his brow, who snores through the night watch. Oh, majesty! When you pinch the man who wears you, you sit on him like rich armor worn in the heat of the day, which scalds him even as it protects him. By his lips there lies a downy feather, and it isn't stirring. If he were breathing, that light, weightless fluff would have to move. My gracious lord, my father! This sleep is deep indeed. It is a sleep that has parted so many English kings from this golden circle. From me you are owed tears and heavy sorrow in the blood, and nature, love and a son's tenderness will pay you those in full, dear father. From you I am owed this royal crown, which comes straight to me from your place and your blood. Look, there it sits. God will guard it, and even if the whole strength of the world were put into one giant arm, it could not force this inheritance from me. I will leave it to my own heirs, just as it is left to me.
[Exit.]
HENRY IV. Warwick! Gloucester! Clarence!
[Enter Warwick, Gloucester, Clarence and the rest.]
CLARENCE. Is the King calling?
WARWICK. What does your Majesty want? How are you, your Grace?
HENRY IV. Why did you leave me here alone, my lords?
CLARENCE. We left the Prince, my brother, here, my liege. He promised to sit and watch over you.
HENRY IV. The Prince of Wales! Where is he? Let me see him. He isn't here.
WARWICK. This door is open. He went out this way.
GLOUCESTER. He didn't come through the room where we were waiting.
HENRY IV. Where is the crown? Who took it from my pillow?
WARWICK. When we left, my liege, we left it here.
HENRY IV. The Prince has taken it away. Go and find him. Is he in such a hurry that he thinks my sleep is my death? Find him, my Lord of Warwick, and scold him back here.
[Exit Warwick.]

This act of his joins with my illness and helps to finish me. Look, my sons, at what creatures you are. See how quickly human nature turns rebel when gold becomes its object! For this, foolish, over-careful fathers have broken their sleep with worry, worn out their brains with care and their bones with toil. For this they have hoarded and piled up heaps of rusting gold won in strange ways. For this they have been careful to train their sons in the arts and in military exercises. Like the bee, we gather the good sweetness from every flower, our thighs packed with wax and our mouths full of honey, and we carry it to the hive. And like the bees, we are murdered for our trouble. This bitter taste is all that his hoarding yields to the father who is dying.
[Enter Warwick.]
Now, where is he, the one who couldn't wait until his friend, sickness, had finished me off?

WARWICK. My lord, I found the Prince in the next room, washing his gentle cheeks with honest tears. He was so deeply sorrowful that even tyranny, which never drank anything but blood, would have washed its knife clean with gentle tears from looking at him. He is coming here now.
HENRY IV. But why did he take the crown away?
[Enter Prince Henry.]
Look, here he comes. Come here to me, Harry. Leave the room, all of you, and let us be alone.
[Exeunt Warwick and the rest.]
PRINCE HENRY. I never thought I would hear you speak again.

HENRY IV. Your wish was father to that thought, Harry. I stay too long with you, and I tire you. Do you hunger so much for my empty chair that you must dress yourself in my honors before your time has come? Oh, foolish youth! You are chasing a greatness that will crush you. Wait just a little. My cloud of dignity is held up by so weak a wind that it will soon fall. My day is growing dim. You have stolen what would have been yours anyway, without any offense, after a few more hours. By taking it, you have sealed up my hopes at my death. Your whole life showed that you did not love me, and now you want me to die certain of it. You hide a thousand daggers in your thoughts, which you have sharpened on your stony heart to stab at the last half hour of my life. What, can you not put up with me for half an hour? Then go, and dig my grave yourself. Tell the merry bells to ring in your ear that you are crowned, not that I am dead. Let every tear that should have watered my hearse be drops of holy oil to anoint your head. Just mix me in with forgotten dust. Give the body that gave you life to the worms. Pull down my officers, break my decrees, for now is the time to mock all formality. Harry the Fifth is crowned. Up with vanity! Down with royal dignity! All you wise counselors, get out! And now let every region send its apes of idleness to the English court! Neighboring countries, purge yourselves of your scum. Do you have a ruffian who will swear, drink, dance, party all night, rob, murder, and commit the oldest sins in the newest ways? Be glad. He will trouble you no more. England will gild his triple guilt twice over. England will give him office, honor and power. For the fifth Harry pulls the muzzle of restraint off his curbed wildness, and the wild dog will sink his teeth into every innocent. Oh, my poor kingdom, sick with civil blows! When my care could not hold back your riots, what will you do when riot is the one in charge? Oh, you will be a wilderness again, peopled with wolves, your old inhabitants!

PRINCE HENRY. Oh, forgive me, my liege! If it were not for my tears, which block my speech, I would have headed off this dear and deep rebuke before you spoke it in grief and I heard it go so far. There is your crown. May He who wears the crown forever keep it yours for a long time! If I want it more than as your honor and your glory, then never let me rise from this kneeling, which my truest and most dutiful spirit teaches my body to do. God is my witness that when I came in here and found no sign of breath in your Majesty, how cold it struck my heart! If I am pretending, oh, let me die in my present wildness and never live to show the doubting world the noble change I have planned! I came to look at you, thinking you dead, and almost dead myself, my liege, from thinking it. I spoke to this crown as if it could hear, and scolded it like this: "The care that hangs on you has fed on my father's body. So you, the best of gold, are the worst of gold. Other gold, less fine in purity, is worth more, because it preserves life when it is dissolved into medicine to drink. But you, the finest, the most honored, the most famous, have eaten up the man who wore you." So, my most royal liege, while accusing it, I put it on my head, to fight with it, as with an enemy that had murdered my father before my face, the quarrel of a true heir. But if it infected my blood with joy, or swelled my thoughts with any kind of pride, if any rebel or vain impulse of mine welcomed its power in even the slightest way, then may God keep it from my head forever, and make me as poor as the poorest servant who kneels to it in awe and terror!

HENRY IV. Oh, my son, God put it in your mind to take it away, so that you would win more of your father's love by pleading so wisely in excuse of it! Come here, Harry, sit by my bed and hear what I think will be the very last advice I will ever speak. God knows, my son, by what by-paths and crooked, indirect ways I came by this crown, and I know well how troublesome it sat on my head. It will pass to you more peacefully, with better reputation and better security, because all the stain of how it was won goes into the earth with me. In me it seemed only an honor snatched with a rough hand. And I had many people alive who reproached me for taking it, with the help of those who supported me. Those quarrels grew daily into bloodshed and wounded what was supposed to be peace. All these bold dangers you see, I have faced at great risk, for my whole reign has been only a play acting out that theme. Now my death changes the tone, because what I got by seizure comes to you in a fairer way. So you wear the garland by succession. Yet though you stand more securely than I could, you are not firm enough, since the wounds are still green. And all my friends, whom you must make your friends, have only just had their stings and teeth pulled out. By their fierce work I was first raised up, and by their power I had good reason to fear being pushed out again. To avoid that, I cut them down, and I now planned to lead many of them to the Holy Land, so that peace and idleness would not make them look too closely at my position. Therefore, my Harry, make it your policy to keep restless minds busy with foreign quarrels, so that this activity, carried abroad, may wear away the memory of earlier days. I would say more, but my lungs are so worn out that I have no strength left to speak. How I came by the crown, oh God, forgive, and grant that it may live in true peace with you!

PRINCE HENRY. My gracious liege, you won it, wore it, kept it, and gave it to me. So my possession must be plain and rightful. With more than ordinary pains, I will rightfully defend it against all the world.
[Enter Lord John of Lancaster and others.]
HENRY IV. Look, look, here comes my John of Lancaster.
LANCASTER. Health, peace and happiness to my royal father!

HENRY IV. You bring me happiness and peace, son John, but health, alas, has flown away on youthful wings from this bare, withered trunk. At the sight of you, my worldly business comes to an end. Where is my Lord of Warwick?
PRINCE HENRY. My Lord of Warwick!
[Enter Warwick and others.]
HENRY IV. Does the room where I first fainted have a particular name?
WARWICK. It's called Jerusalem, my noble lord.

HENRY IV. Praise be to God! My life must end right there. It was prophesied to me many years ago that I would die only in Jerusalem, which I foolishly supposed meant the Holy Land. But carry me to that chamber. I'll lie there. In that Jerusalem Harry shall die.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Gloucestershire. Shallow’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Shallow, Falstaff, Bardolph and Page.]
SHALLOW. By cock and pie, sir, you won't leave tonight. What, Davy, I say!
FALSTAFF. You must excuse me, Master Robert Shallow.
SHALLOW. I will not excuse you. You will not be excused. No excuses will be accepted, no excuse will do, you will not be excused. Why, Davy!
[Enter Davy.]
DAVY. Here, sir.
SHALLOW. Davy, Davy, Davy, Davy, let me see, Davy, let me see, Davy, let me see. Yes, indeed, William the cook. Tell him to come here. Sir John, you will not be excused.
DAVY. Well, sir, it's like this: those summonses can't be served. And another thing, sir, shall we sow the headland with wheat?
SHALLOW. With red wheat, Davy. But about William the cook, are there no young pigeons?
DAVY. Yes, sir. Here is the blacksmith's bill for shoeing and plough-irons.
SHALLOW. Add it up and pay it. Sir John, you will not be excused.
DAVY. Now, sir, the bucket needs a new link. And, sir, do you mean to dock any of William's wages for the sack of grain he lost the other day at Hinckley fair?
SHALLOW. He shall answer for it. Some pigeons, Davy, a couple of short-legged hens, a joint of mutton, and any pretty little fancy dishes. Tell William the cook.
DAVY. Is the man of war staying all night, sir?
SHALLOW. Yes, Davy, I will treat him well. A friend at court is better than a penny in the purse. Treat his men well, Davy, for they are out-and-out rogues and will gossip behind your back.
DAVY. No worse than they get gossiped about, sir, for they have terribly filthy linen.
SHALLOW. Well put, Davy. Get on with your business, Davy.
DAVY. I beg you, sir, to favor William Visor of Woncot against Clement Perkes of the hill.
SHALLOW. There are many complaints against that Visor, Davy. That Visor is an out-and-out rogue, as I know.

DAVY. I grant your worship that he is a rogue, sir, but God forbid, sir, that a rogue should get no favor at his friend's request. An honest man, sir, can speak for himself when a rogue can't. I have served your worship faithfully, sir, these eight years. And if I can't once or twice a quarter stand up for a rogue against an honest man, then I have very little credit with your worship. The rogue is my honest friend, sir. So I beg your worship, let him be favored.
SHALLOW. Go on; I say he shall have no wrong. Look to things, Davy.
[Exit Davy.]
Where are you, Sir John? Come, come, come, off with your boots. Give me your hand, Master Bardolph.
BARDOLPH. I'm glad to see your worship.
SHALLOW. I thank you with all my heart, kind Master Bardolph. And welcome, my fine fellow [_to the Page_]. Come, Sir John.
FALSTAFF. I'll follow you, good Master Robert Shallow.
[Exit Shallow.]
Bardolph, look after our horses.
[Exeunt Bardolph and Page.]

If I were sawed into pieces, I could make four dozen bearded walking-sticks like Master Shallow, each one a hermit's staff. It's a wonderful thing to see how closely his servants' spirits match his own. By watching him, they behave like foolish justices. By talking with them, he has turned into a servant who plays the justice. Their spirits are so married together by living side by side that they flock together in agreement, like so many wild geese. If I wanted a favor from Master Shallow, I would flatter his men by suggesting they were close to their master. If I wanted a favor from his men, I would butter up Master Shallow by saying no man could command his servants better. It's certain that people catch wise behavior or ignorant behavior from each other, the way they catch diseases. So men should watch the company they keep. I will make up enough material out of this Shallow to keep Prince Harry laughing continually for as long as it takes to wear out six fashions, which is four law terms, or two lawsuits, and he will laugh without a break. Oh, it's amazing what a lie with a mild oath and a joke with a straight face can do to a fellow who has never had an ache in his shoulders! Oh, you will see him laugh until his face is like a wet cloak badly folded away!
SHALLOW.
[Within.] Sir John!
FALSTAFF. I'm coming, Master Shallow, I'm coming, Master Shallow.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — Westminster. The palace
paragraphs: [Enter Warwick and the Lord Chief Justice, meeting.]
WARWICK. Well, my Lord Chief Justice, where are you going?
CHIEF JUSTICE. How is the King?
WARWICK. Very well. All his cares are over now.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I hope he's not dead.
WARWICK. He has walked the road of nature, and for our purposes he lives no more.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I wish his Majesty had called me along with him. The service I truly did for his life has left me open to every injury.
WARWICK. Indeed, I think the young King doesn't love you.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I know he doesn't, and I am arming myself to meet the state of things, which cannot look more hideous to me than I have already pictured it in my imagination.
[Enter Lancaster, Clarence, Gloucester and others.]

WARWICK. Here come the grieving sons of dead Harry. Oh, if only the living Harry had the temperament of even the worst of these three gentlemen! Then how many nobles would keep their places, who must now lower their sails to base sorts of men!
CHIEF JUSTICE. Oh God, I fear everything will be overturned.
LANCASTER. Good morning, cousin Warwick, good morning.
GLOUCESTER & CLARENCE. Good morning, cousin.
LANCASTER. We meet like men who have forgotten how to speak.
WARWICK. We remember how, but our subject is too heavy to allow much talk.
LANCASTER. Well, peace be with him who has made us heavy-hearted!
CHIEF JUSTICE. Peace be with us, so that we don't become heavier!
GLOUCESTER. Oh, my good lord, you have lost a friend indeed. And I dare swear that you didn't borrow that face of seeming sorrow. It is surely your own.
LANCASTER. Though no man can be sure what favor he will find, you stand in the coldest expectation. I am the sorrier for it, and wish it were otherwise.
CLARENCE. Well, you must now speak politely to Sir John Falstaff, which goes against the current of your rank.

CHIEF JUSTICE. Sweet Princes, what I did, I did in honor, led by the fair guidance of my conscience. And you will never see me beg for a ragged, pardon pleaded for in advance. If truth and upright innocence fail me, I'll go to the King my master, who is dead, and tell him who sent me after him.
WARWICK. Here comes the Prince.
[Enter King Henry the Fifth, attended.]
CHIEF JUSTICE. Good morning, and God save your Majesty!

HENRY V. This new and gorgeous garment, majesty, doesn't sit as easily on me as you think. Brothers, you mix your sadness with some fear. This is the English court, not the Turkish one. Here it is not one Amurath succeeding another, but Harry succeeding Harry. Yet be sad, good brothers, for, on my faith, it suits you very well. Sorrow looks so royal in you that I will take up the fashion deeply and wear it in my heart. So be sad, but take on no more of it, good brothers, than a burden we all share. As for me, by heaven, I promise you, I'll be your father and your brother too. Just give me your love and I'll carry your cares. Weep for the death of Harry, and so will I. But Harry lives on, and he will turn those tears, one by one, into hours of happiness.
PRINCES. We hope for nothing else from your Majesty.
HENRY V. You all look at me strangely. And you most of all. I think you are sure that I don't love you.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I am sure that, if I am judged rightly, your Majesty has no just cause to hate me.

HENRY V. No? How could a prince with my great hopes forget the great indignities you heaped on me? What! To rebuke and scold the immediate heir of England, and roughly send him to prison? Was that a small thing? Can it be washed away in Lethe and forgotten?

CHIEF JUSTICE. I was then acting in your father's person. The image of his power lay in me then. And while I was busy administering his law for the good of the commonwealth, your Highness chose to forget my office, the majesty and power of law and justice, and the image of the King whom I represented, and struck me in my very seat of judgment. For that, as an offender against your father, I gave bold way to my authority and committed you to prison. If the deed was wrong, then answer this, now that you wear the garland: would you be content to have a son of yours set your decrees at nothing? To pull justice down from your awesome bench? To trip up the course of law and blunt the sword that guards the peace and safety of your own person? Even more, to kick at your most royal image and mock your actions as they are carried out in a second body? Question your royal thoughts and make the case your own. Be the father now, and picture a son. Hear your own dignity so profaned, see your most dreadful laws so loosely brushed aside, watch yourself so scorned by a son. Then imagine me taking your part and, in your power, quietly silencing your son. After this cool consideration, pass sentence on me. And as you are a king, say with royal authority what I did that was unbecoming to my office, my person, or my king's sovereignty.

HENRY V. You are right, justice, and you weigh this well. Therefore keep on carrying the scales and the sword. And I wish your honors may increase until you live to see a son of mine offend you and obey you, as I did. Then I shall live to say my father's words: "I am happy to have a man so bold that he dares to do justice on my own son. And I am no less happy to have a son who would hand his greatness over so willingly into the hands of justice." You committed me to prison, and for that I now commit into your hand the unstained sword that you have carried, with this reminder: use it with the same bold, just and impartial spirit that you showed against me. Here is my hand. You shall be a father to my youth. My voice will say what you whisper in my ear, and I will bow down and humble my intentions to your wise, well-practiced guidance. And, princes all, believe me, I beg you, my father has gone wild into his grave, for my own wild desires lie in his tomb. And with his spirit I sadly live on, to mock the world's expectations, to frustrate prophecies, and to wipe out the rotten opinion that has written me down according to how I seemed. The tide of blood in me has flowed proudly in vanity until now. Now it turns and ebbs back to the sea, where it will mingle with the great waters and from now on flow in formal majesty. Now let us call our high court of parliament, and let us choose such members of noble counsel that the great body of our state may march in equal rank with the best-governed nation. Then war, or peace, or both at once, will be things we know and are familiar with. In this, father, you shall have the foremost hand. When our coronation is done, we will summon, as I said before, all our nobility. And, if God grants my good intentions, no prince or peer will have just cause to say, "God shorten Harry's happy life by one day!"
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — Gloucestershire. Shallow’s orchard
paragraphs: [Enter Falstaff, Shallow, Silence, Davy, Bardolph and the Page.]
SHALLOW. No, you must see my orchard, where we'll eat a last year's pippin apple of my own grafting in an arbor, with a dish of caraway seeds and so on. Come, cousin Silence. And then to bed.
FALSTAFF. By God, you have a fine dwelling here, and a rich one.
SHALLOW. Barren, barren, barren. We're all beggars, all beggars, Sir John. Well, the air is good. Lay the table, Davy, lay the table, Davy. Well done, Davy.
FALSTAFF. This Davy serves you in many useful ways. He is your servant and your husbandman.
SHALLOW. A good fellow, a good fellow, a very good fellow, Sir John. By the mass, I drank too much sack at supper. A good fellow. Now sit down, now sit down. Come, cousin.
SILENCE. Ah, my lad! says he, we shall [_Singing._]
Do nothing but eat, and make good cheer, and praise God for the merry year, when flesh is cheap and women dear, and lusty lads roam here and there so merrily, and ever among so merrily.
FALSTAFF. There's a merry heart! Good Master Silence, I'll drink your health for that soon.
SHALLOW. Give Master Bardolph some wine, Davy.

DAVY. Sweet sir, sit down. I'll be with you soon. Most sweet sir, sit down. Master page, good master page, sit down. Much good may it do you! What you lack in food, we'll make up in drink, but you must put up with it. The heart is what counts.
[Exit.]
SHALLOW. Be merry, Master Bardolph, and you too, my little soldier there, be merry.
SILENCE.
[Singing.]
_Be merry, be merry, my wife has all, For women are shrews, both short and tall. 'Tis merry in hall when beards wag all, And welcome merry Shrove-tide. Be merry, be merry._
FALSTAFF. I never thought Master Silence was a man of such spirit.
SILENCE. Who, me? I've been merry twice and once before now.
[Enter Davy.]
DAVY.
[_To Bardolph_.] Here's a dish of russet apples for you.
SHALLOW. Davy!
DAVY. Your worship? I'll be with you right away.
[To Bardolph.] A cup of wine, sir?
SILENCE.
[Singing.]
_A cup of wine that's brisk and fine, And drink unto thee, leman mine, And a merry heart lives long-a._
FALSTAFF. Well sung, Master Silence.
SILENCE. If we are to be merry, now comes the sweet part of the night.
FALSTAFF. Health and long life to you, Master Silence.
SILENCE.
[Singing.]
_Fill the cup, and let it come, I'll pledge you a mile to th' bottom._

SHALLOW. Honest Bardolph, welcome! If you want anything and don't ask for it, curse your heart. Welcome, my little tiny thief, [_to the Page_] and welcome indeed too. I'll drink to Master Bardolph, and to all the gallants around London.
DAVY. I hope to see London once before I die.
BARDOLPH. If I could see you there, Davy,—
SHALLOW. By the mass, you'd crack a quart together, ha! Wouldn't you, Master Bardolph?
BARDOLPH. Yes, sir, in a two-quart pot.
SHALLOW. By God's life, I thank you. The rogue will stick by you, I can assure you of that. He won't quit, he won't. He's true bred.
BARDOLPH. And I'll stick by him, sir.
SHALLOW. Why, there spoke a king. Lack for nothing! Be merry.
[Knocking within.]
Look who's at the door there, ho! Who's knocking?
[Exit Davy.]
FALSTAFF.
[To Silence, seeing him take off a bumper.] Why, now you have done me
right.
SILENCE.
[Singing.]
Do me right, and dub me knight: Samingo.
Isn't it so?
FALSTAFF. It is so.
SILENCE. Is it so? Why then, let it be said that an old man can do something.
[Enter Davy.]
DAVY. If it please your worship, there's a man named Pistol come from the court with news.
FALSTAFF. From the court? Let him come in.
[Enter Pistol.]
How now, Pistol?
PISTOL. Sir John, God save you!
FALSTAFF. What wind blew you here, Pistol?
PISTOL. Not the ill wind that blows no man any good. Sweet knight, you are now one of the greatest men in this realm.
SILENCE. By Our Lady, I think he is, except for goodman Puff of Barson.

PISTOL. Puff! Puff in your teeth, you most cowardly, base wretch! Sir John, I am your Pistol and your friend. I have ridden helter-skelter to you, and I bring tidings, lucky joys, golden times, and happy news of great price.
FALSTAFF. Please, now, deliver them like a man of this world.
PISTOL. A foutre for the world and its base worldlings! I speak of Africa and golden joys.
FALSTAFF. Oh, base Assyrian knight, what is your news? Let King Cophetua know the truth of it.
SILENCE.
[Singing.] And Robin Hood, Scarlet, and John.
PISTOL. Shall dunghill curs stand up to the Helicons? And shall good news be baffled? Then, Pistol, lay your head in the Furies' lap.
SHALLOW. Honest gentleman, I don't know your breeding.
PISTOL. Why then, lament for it.
SHALLOW. Pardon me, sir. If you come with news from the court, I take it there are only two ways: either to tell it, or to keep it back. I am, sir, a man of some authority under the King.
PISTOL. Under which king, you beggar? Speak, or die.
SHALLOW. Under King Harry.
PISTOL. Harry the Fourth, or Fifth?
SHALLOW. Harry the Fourth.
PISTOL. A foutre for your office! Sir John, your tender lambkin is now King. Harry the Fifth is the man. I speak the truth. When Pistol lies, do this, and fig me, like the bragging Spaniard.
FALSTAFF. What, is the old King dead?
PISTOL. Dead as a doornail. What I say is just.
FALSTAFF. Away, Bardolph, saddle my horse. Master Robert Shallow, choose whatever office you like in the land, it's yours. Pistol, I will load you with double honors.
BARDOLPH. Oh, joyful day! I wouldn't trade this for a knighthood.
PISTOL. What! I do bring good news.
FALSTAFF. Carry Master Silence to bed. Master Shallow, my Lord Shallow, be whatever you like. I am Fortune's steward! Get your boots on, we'll ride all night. Oh, sweet Pistol! Away, Bardolph!
[Exit Bardolph.]

Come, Pistol, tell me more. And meanwhile think of something to do for your own good. Boots, boots, Master Shallow. I know the young King is sick for me. Let's take anybody's horses. The laws of England are at my command. Blessed are those who have been my friends, and woe to my Lord Chief Justice!
PISTOL. Let vile vultures tear out his lungs too! "Where is the life that late I led?" they say. Why, here it is. Welcome these pleasant days!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — London. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Beadles, dragging in Hostess Quickly and Doll Tearsheet.]
HOSTESS. No, you out-and-out rogue. I wish to God I could die, so that I could have you hanged. You have pulled my shoulder out of joint.
FIRST BEADLE. The constables have handed her over to me, and I guarantee she'll get plenty of whipping-cheer. A man or two have been killed over her lately.

DOLL. Nut-hook, nut-hook, you liar! Come on, I'll tell you what, you damned tripe-faced rascal. If the child I'm carrying now miscarries, you'd have been better off hitting your own mother, you paper-faced villain.
HOSTESS. Oh Lord, if only Sir John would come! He would make this a bloody day for somebody. But I pray God the fruit of her womb miscarries!

FIRST BEADLE. If it does, you'll have a dozen cushions again. You only have eleven now, because the twelfth is stuffed under your dress as the baby. Come, I order you both to come with me, because the man you and Pistol beat between you is dead.

DOLL. I'll tell you what, you thin man in a censer, I'll have you thoroughly flogged for this, you bluebottle rogue, you filthy starved executioner. If you aren't flogged, I'll give up wearing half-skirts.
FIRST BEADLE. Come, come, you she knight-errant, come.
HOSTESS. Oh God, that right should be beaten by might like this! Well, from suffering comes ease.
DOLL. Come, you rogue, come, take me to a justice.
HOSTESS. Yes, come, you starved bloodhound.
DOLL. Goodman Death, goodman Bones!
HOSTESS. You skeleton, you!
DOLL. Come, you thin thing, come, you rascal!
FIRST BEADLE. Very well.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — A public place near Westminster Abbey
paragraphs: [Enter two Grooms, strewing rushes.]
FIRST GROOM. More rushes! Bring more rushes!
SECOND GROOM. The trumpets have already sounded twice.
FIRST GROOM. It will be two o'clock before they get back from the coronation. Hurry, hurry.
[Exeunt.]
[Trumpets sound, and the King and his train pass over the stage. Enter Falstaff, Shallow, Pistol, Bardolph and Page.]
FALSTAFF. Stand here beside me, Master Robert Shallow. I'll make the King show you favor. I'll give him a look as he passes, and you just watch the face he gives me.
PISTOL. God bless your lungs, good knight!

FALSTAFF. Come here, Pistol, and stand behind me. Oh, if I'd had time to make new uniforms, I'd have spent on them the thousand pounds I borrowed from you. But it doesn't matter. This shabby show is better. It proves how eager I was to see him.
SHALLOW. It does indeed.
FALSTAFF. It shows how warmly I feel for him—
SHALLOW. It does indeed.
FALSTAFF. My devotion—
SHALLOW. It does, it does, it does.
FALSTAFF. So that I rode day and night, without stopping to think, or remember, or even have the patience to change my clothes—
SHALLOW. That's best, certainly.
FALSTAFF. But just stand here, stained with travel and sweating with longing to see him. I thought of nothing else, and forgot every other matter, as if there were nothing to do but see him.
PISTOL. It's _semper idem_, "always the same," for _obsque hoc nihil est_, "without this there is nothing": it's all in every part.
SHALLOW. It is so, indeed.

PISTOL. My knight, I will fire up your noble liver and make you rage. Your Doll, the Helen of your noble thoughts, is in a vile and plague-ridden prison. She was dragged there by a common, dirty hand. Rouse up revenge from the black den, with fierce Alecto's snake, for Doll is locked up. Pistol speaks nothing but the truth.
FALSTAFF. I'll set her free.
[Shouts within. The trumpets sound.]
PISTOL. There the sea roared, and the trumpets' clang sounds out.
[Enter the King and his train, the Lord Chief Justice among them.]
FALSTAFF. God save your Grace, King Hal, my royal Hal!
PISTOL. May the heavens guard and keep you, most royal child of fame!
FALSTAFF. God save you, my sweet boy!
HENRY V. My Lord Chief Justice, speak to that foolish man.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Are you in your right mind? Do you know what you're saying?
FALSTAFF. My King! My Jove! I'm speaking to you, my heart!

HENRY V. I don't know you, old man. Go and say your prayers. How badly white hair suits a fool and a jester! For a long time I dreamed of a man like you, so swollen with overeating, so old, and so profane. But now that I'm awake, I despise my dream. Make your body smaller from now on, and your soul greater. Give up gorging yourself. Know that the grave gapes three times wider for you than for other men. Don't answer me with a fool's joke. Don't presume that I am the man I was. God knows, and the world will see, that I have turned away my former self. I will turn away those who kept me company in it. When you hear that I am as I used to be, come to me, and you will be what you were: the tutor and the feeder of my wild living. Until then I banish you, on pain of death, as I have banished the rest of those who led me astray. You are not to come within ten miles of my person. I will allow you enough to live on, so that lack of money does not force you into evil. And as we hear that you are reforming yourselves, we will promote you, according to your abilities and qualities. My lord, it is your duty to see that the terms of my word are carried out. Move on.
[Exeunt King with his train.]
FALSTAFF. Master Shallow, I owe you a thousand pounds.
SHALLOW. Yes, indeed, Sir John, and I beg you to let me take it home with me.

FALSTAFF. That can hardly be done, Master Shallow. Don't let this upset you. He'll send for me in private. You see, he has to put on this face for the world. Don't worry about your promotion. I'll still be the man who makes you great.
SHALLOW. I can't see how, unless you give me your jacket and stuff me with straw. Please, good Sir John, let me have five hundred of my thousand.
FALSTAFF. Sir, I'll be as good as my word. What you just heard was only a pretense.
SHALLOW. A pretense that I fear you'll die in, Sir John.
FALSTAFF. Don't fear pretenses. Come to dinner with me. Come, Lieutenant Pistol; come, Bardolph. I'll be sent for soon, tonight.
[Enter the Lord Chief Justice and Prince John, Officers with them.]
CHIEF JUSTICE. Go, take Sir John Falstaff to the Fleet prison. Take all his company along with him.
FALSTAFF. My lord, my lord,—
CHIEF JUSTICE. I can't speak now. I'll hear you soon. Take them away.
PISTOL. _Si fortuna me tormenta, spero me contenta._ If fortune torments me, I hope to be content.
[Exeunt all but Prince John and the Lord Chief Justice.]

LANCASTER. I like this fair way the King has handled things. He means for his old followers to be well provided for. But they are all banished until their way of life looks wiser and more modest to the world.
CHIEF JUSTICE. And so they are.
LANCASTER. The King has called his parliament, my lord.
CHIEF JUSTICE. He has.

LANCASTER. I'll bet that before this year is over, we will carry our civil swords and native fire as far as France. I heard a little bird sing so, and its music, I think, pleased the King. Come, will you go?
[Exeunt.]
EPILOGUE.

First my fear, then my curtsy, last my speech. My fear is your displeasure; my curtsy is my duty; and my speech is to beg your pardon. If you're expecting a good speech now, you ruin me, because what I have to say is my own making, and what I really ought to say will, I suspect, turn out to be my own undoing. But to the point, and so to the risk. You should know, as you well do, that I was here recently at the end of a displeasing play, to ask for your patience and to promise you a better one. I meant to pay you with this one. If, like a bad venture, it comes home unlucky, I go bankrupt, and you, my kind creditors, lose. Here I promised I would be, and here I give my body into your mercy. Let me off some of the debt, and I will pay you the rest. And like most debtors, I'll promise you endlessly.

If my tongue can't persuade you to let me off, will you order me to use my legs? And yet that would be a light payment, to dance out of your debt. But a clear conscience will make any payment it possibly can, and so would I. All the ladies here have forgiven me. If the gentlemen won't, then the gentlemen disagree with the ladies, which was never seen before in such an audience.

One more word, I beg you. If you aren't too stuffed with rich food, our humble author will continue the story, with Sir John in it, and make you merry with fair Katharine of France. There, for all I know, Falstaff will die of a sweat, unless he's already been killed by your harsh opinions. For Oldcastle died a martyr, and this is not the man. My tongue is tired. When my legs are too, I will say good night to you.
